items.title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Synchronize adaptive DSpark decisions across TP ranks
items.body:
This carries #56831 by @CedricHwong forward to current main. That PR has been idle since 09-14 and no longer passes CI after the rebase. Cedric's commit is kept unchanged, with his authorship. The two commits on top address the review comments on that PR.

Adaptive verification (DSpark) picks the per-step draft budget on the host from rank-local stale confidences, then picks which slots to keep on the device from rank-local live confidences. If TP ranks disagree on either one, they run different batch layouts: different token counts, or equal totals with different request boundaries. That breaks the collectives that follow and can hang them (#54011). This PR makes TP rank 0 authoritative:

1. `get_num_tokens`: `draft_budget` is broadcast with `broadcast_object` (shm MessageQueue, host only).
2. `reallocate_drafts`: on steps that trim, the per-request `capacities` are broadcast from rank 0 before `cu_num_logits` / `query_start_loc` are built.

Both conditions around (2), `draft_budget == 0` and `draft_budget < scheduled drafts`, depend only on the broadcast budget and scheduler-provided counts. Every TP rank therefore takes the same branch, and the collective cannot be entered unevenly.

### Changes vs #56831

- **Test updates for current main.** #56888 renamed `async_copy_to_gpu` to `async_tensor_h2d`; the old monkeypatch no longer resolved, giving 12 failures, and `cpu.yaml` runs `-x`. #55939 made `tests/v1/spec_decode` type-checked, so the test now narrows `_batch_budget` before indexing it.
- **`capacities` now goes over the TP group's PyNCCL communicator when it is enabled**, and falls back to `GroupCoordinator.broadcast` otherwise (`VLLM_DISABLE_PYNCCL`, XPU, CPU).
  - **Why not `GroupCoordinator.broadcast`:** it uses `torch.distributed` on the device group. On CUDA no other TP collective touches that group, and vLLM passes no `device_id`, so its NCCL communicator would be created on the first trimmed serving step, after the KV cache was sized. Measured on MI355X with a cold device group: +105 ms / +1.0 GiB per GPU at TP2, and +224 ms / +1.7-1.8 GiB per GPU at TP4.
  - **Why not `device_communicator.broadcast`:** it raises when PyNCCL is disabled on CUDA, and on XPU it passes the group-local `src` where torch expects a global rank.
  - **Speed:** PyNCCL is also faster per call: about 6 us vs 32 us host enqueue, and 12-14 us vs 25-26 us GPU time.
- A test case covers the PyNCCL-disabled fallback.

Scope: this covers TP, which also covers DCP. With PCP > 1, each PCP rank's TP group has its own leader, and AV + PCP is not gated today; that is a follow-up.

## Test Plan

- `pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py`, plus `mypy` / `ruff` via the pre-commit pins.
- Multi-rank CPU harness: real gloo groups, the real `GroupCoordinator` and the real `AdaptiveVerificationManager`. TP 2/4/8, with injected per-rank confidence drift from 1 ULP to large.
- MI355X microbenchmark of both collectives, using vLLM's real TP group (`init_distributed_environment` + `initialize_model_parallel`) at TP2/TP4.
- MI355X end to end:
  - Model: Qwen3-4B + `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` with `enable_adaptive_verification: true`, V2 model runner, ROCM_ATTN.
  - Workload: 600 GSM8K CoT prompts, output 512, greedy.
  - A/B: main vs this PR, conc 1/16/64, 4 interleaved rounds per arm.
  - Divergence check: an instrumented main that all-gathers every rank's locally computed budget, capacities and confidences on every step.

## Test Result

- **Unit tests:** 49 passed. mypy and ruff are clean. With both collectives removed, the 9 TP>1 cases that need consensus fail.
- **Multi-rank harness:** 0 mismatches on this branch at every world size and drift level.
  - Without the fix, a single fp32 ULP is enough to change the layout. Mismatching steps per 1000 at TP 2/4/8 (capacities or boundaries):
    - 1-16 ULP: 0-2
    - 1e-4 relative: 2-9
    - 1e-2 relative: 65-382
  - Most mismatches have equal totals across ranks but different request boundaries.
- **Per-step cost, MI355X, p50 (p90), slowest rank:**

| | TP2 | TP4 |
|---|---|---|
| `broadcast_object(budget)`: every step that has drafts, host only | 6.7 us (7.5) | 7.9 us (8.2) |
| `capacities` broadcast: trimmed steps only. Host enqueue + in-stream GPU time; does not depend on num_reqs from 1 to 256 | 6.2 + 12.4 us | 6.5 + 14.0 us |
| Worst-case total for a trimmed step, with no overlap | ~25 us | ~29 us (p90 ~32) |

  That is 0.2-0.6% of a 5-15 ms decode step, about the cost of two of the TP all-reduces each step already does. With the original `GroupCoordinator.broadcast`, a trimmed step costs about 64-68 us.
- **End to end at TP2: no measurable regression.** Each delta is within about 1.2 standard deviations; run-to-run CV is 0.2-0.6%.

| conc | output tok/s, main | output tok/s, this PR | delta | TPOT p50, main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 721.0 ± 4.1 | 727.7 ± 10 | +0.9% | 1.311 → 1.314 ms |
| 16 | 5489 ± 12 | 5493 ± 15 | +0.1% | 2.755 → 2.763 ms |
| 64 | 10590 ± 50 | 10585 ± 19 | -0.1% | 5.615 → 5.629 ms |

  Acceptance length is unchanged (±0.7%). There were 0 failed requests in 24 runs. The `capacities` broadcast fired on about 97% of c16/c64 steps and about 7% of c1 steps.
- **Natural divergence was not observed on this setup.**
  - Instrumented main ran 8434 steps at TP2 and 7886 steps at TP4: 0 budget, capacities or confidence mismatches.
  - A separate DeepSeek-V4.1 TP4 MI355X serving trace ran about 478k AV steps, also with 0 mismatches.
  - Here the confidence inputs are bitwise identical across ranks, because the custom all-reduce sums in a fixed rank order. Divergence needs rank-asymmetric numerics, such as rank-order-dependent reductions, non-deterministic kernels, or the TP8 H20 DeepSeek-V4 setup in #54011.
  - The fix is cheap insurance against that: per the numbers above, about 7 us host per step plus about 19 us per trimmed step.

Co-authored with @CedricHwong (original fix, #56831). Supersedes #56831.

items.title: [Spec Decode] Fix Dspark adaptive verification cost model
items.body:
## Summary

Adaptive verification picks, every step, the draft budget `b` that maximises

```
expected accepted tokens(b) / step cost(b)
step cost(b) = drafter cost + base + (price of b draft slots)
```

The argmax depends only on how the slot price compares with the base. The current cost model gets both wrong, because it reads everything off a single profiled curve. This PR profiles the two separately and prices the base from the batch's real shape and context.

On Qwen3-4B with DSpark at batch size 256 (TP1, H100), this gives **+2.7% output throughput on SPEED-Bench throughput_1k** and **+8.4% on MT-Bench**. The fixed model won all 10 paired runs.

## The bug

`batches_to_profile` ran one family of dummy batches: *n* requests, one token each, every request carrying `VLLM_ADAPTIVE_VERIFICATION_PROFILE_CONTEXT_LEN` (default 8192) tokens of fabricated KV context. That produced `verify_cost_ms[n]`, whose index means *n sequences, each reading 8k tokens of KV*. `get_num_tokens` then priced every budget as

```python
costs = draft_cost_ms[num_reqs] + verify_cost_ms[num_non_draft_tokens : num_non_draft_tokens + max_draft_budget + 1]
```

That one lookup has three errors.

1. **A draft slot is priced as another whole sequence with 8k of context.** Walking `b` steps along `verify_cost_ms` charges each draft token as one more request reading 8k of KV. A draft slot is really one more query token on a sequence already in the batch, so it reads no new KV.
2. **The base always assumes 8k of context per request.** Workloads with short contexts, such as MT-Bench, carry a few hundred tokens, so most of the base's attention cost is fictional.
3. **The base is looked up by token count on a request-count axis.** `num_non_draft_tokens` counts tokens, but the curve is indexed by requests at one token each. With chunked prefill in the step, every prefill token is charged as an extra 8k-context sequence.

### Example (Qwen3-4B, H100)

Qwen3-4B stores 36 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dims × 2 (K and V) × 2 bytes = 144 KiB of KV per token, so one 8k-context sequence reads about 1.2 GB of KV per step.

- **Draft slot (error 1).** Take 64 decoding requests, each with 7 drafts. The old model prices draft slot 1 as `verify_cost_ms[65] - verify_cost_ms[64]`, which is one more 8k-context sequence. At ~3.3 TB/s that is roughly **0.36 ms per slot** of KV read alone. The draft-axis profile in this PR measures the real price at **10.4–11.7 µs per slot** on the same GPU, about 30× lower. At long context the old model therefore declines draft slots that would have paid for themselves.
- **Base (errors 2 and 3).** Take 256 MT-Bench requests decoding at ~400 tokens of context. The old base prices 256 × 8k × 144 KiB ≈ 300 GB of KV reads (tens of ms). The batch really reads 256 × 400 × 144 KiB ≈ 15 GB. With the base overstated by an order of magnitude, every draft slot looks nearly free relative to the step. The sizer then buys slots whose acceptance doesn't justify them. A step that also carries a 190-token prefill chunk is charged as 190 more 8k-context sequences instead.

## The fix

**Profiling** (`batches_to_profile`, `set_initial_cost_curves`):

- The one-token-per-request pass at the profiled context runs as before and still produces `verify_cost_ms`.
- A second pass runs the same shapes with **no fabricated context**. Samples now record their context (`StepTimingSample.context_len`, set by `StepTimingCollector.record_batch` only while collecting), so the two passes are never pooled.
- **Draft-axis probes** run at each captured request count with the full query length `K + 1`. `_dummy_run` takes a `num_reqs` kwarg so the request count stays fixed while tokens grow.

Three new curves come out of these passes:

- `slope_curve`: price of one draft slot by request count. It is the rise from a one-token-per-request step to a full-query step at the same request count, divided by the slots added. Everything that depends only on the request count (weights, KV reads, launch overhead) cancels in the difference.
- `token_curve`: step cost by token count with no KV context. This covers matmuls, the padding staircase, and the loss of CUDA graphs past the capture limit.
- `kv_curve`: price of reading one context token, by request count. It is computed as (with-context step − no-context step) / (requests × context).

**Runtime** (`_budget_costs_ms`, called from `get_num_tokens`). For a batch of `R` requests running `N` non-draft tokens with `C = sum(num_computed_tokens)` tokens of context:

```
base        = token_table[N] + kv_table[R] * C
cost(b)     = drafter[R] + base + slot_table[R] * b          if N + b <= capture limit
```

**Past the CUDA-graph capture limit.** The formula above is linear in `b`, but the real step cost is not. Once `N + b` exceeds the largest captured size (`max_cudagraph_capture_size`), the target forward stops replaying a full CUDA graph and runs piecewise or eager. That adds a one-time jump in cost at the limit, and past it the cost grows with the step's token count at the ungraphed rate. A constant per-slot price can't represent either. Without a correction, the sizer would see no cliff and push budgets across the limit as if they were as cheap as the graphed ones.

The old single curve did contain this cliff, because it was indexed by total token count. Splitting the cost into a base plus a per-slot price would lose it, so `_budget_costs_ms` restores it from the context-free token table. That table is profiled on both sides of the limit: the captured sizes, then tail sizes at 1.5× and doubling up to `max_num_batched_tokens`, which run piecewise or eager. It is interpolated only between points on the same side of the limit. For budgets that cross the limit:

```
fixed       = drafter[R] + kv_table[R] * C                  # parts drafts don't change
linear(b)   = fixed + token_table[N] + slot_table[R] * b    # the formula above
cost(b)     = max(linear(b), fixed + token_table[N + b])    if N + b > capture limit
```

The context-dependent KV read and the drafter cost are kept as they are. Only the token-count term is re-looked-up at the step's real size `N + b`, which picks up the graph-loss jump and the ungraphed per-token rate. Taking the `max` means an ungraphed budget is never priced below the linear estimate. The token table has no context behind its requests, so on its own it can undercount the extra attention that the draft slots do.

For example, Qwen3-4B at batch size 256 captures sizes up to 512, and 256 decoding requests give `N = 256`. Budgets `b <= 256` stay inside the graphs and use the linear price of about 11 µs per slot. From `b = 257` on, the step is 513+ tokens, and `cost(b)` takes the jump to the ungraphed token-table price. The sizer therefore verifies more than 256 drafts only when the extra expected acceptance pays for losing the graph, not just for the slots.

Everything at runtime is host-side numpy over arrays the runner already holds, so the fix adds no device syncs. The memory-profiling capture pass samples only the largest graphs, so it has no draft-axis shape to probe. That pass leaves slots unpriced, and the real capture pass reprofiles. A warning fires only if probes ran and still produced no price. The profiled tables are logged at debug level (`DSpark cost tables: ...`).

## Tradeoffs and limitations

- **Startup time.** The context-free pass and the draft-axis probes add about 20 s of profiling on Qwen3-4B at batch size 256: the graph-capture phase goes from about 30 s to 50 s. Per step, the added cost is one numpy sum over the batch.
- **Linear slot price inside the graphed range.** Within the captured sizes, a slot's cost is a constant per request count. Padding steps between captured sizes are not modelled per slot.

## Results

Setup:

- Model and hardware: Qwen3-4B with `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` (`num_speculative_tokens` 7), adaptive verification on, TP1 on one H100 80GB.
- Batching: `--max-num-seqs 256`, `--max-concurrency 256`, about 250 requests running and 0 waiting throughout.
- Requests: 1,280 per run, T=0, output up to 512 tokens or EOS, prefix caching off, chat endpoint with `enable_thinking=false`.
- Repeats: 5 per dataset. Each pair ran on the same GPU, alternating which variant ran first.

| Dataset | Before (tok/s) | After (tok/s) | Speedup | Per-pair speedup | Acceptance length (before / after) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPEED-Bench throughput_1k | 9,898 (sd 41) | 10,165 (sd 41) | **+2.7%** | +2.3, +3.2, +3.2, +2.2, +2.7% | 3.38 / 3.37 |
| MT-Bench (80 first-turn prompts, oversampled to 1,280) | 22,198 (sd 190) | 24,072 (sd 268) | **+8.4%** | +7.4, +8.3, +8.2, +8.8, +9.4% | 3.77 / 3.67 |

MT-Bench gains the most because its contexts are the furthest from the 8k the old base assumed. Acceptance length drops slightly while throughput rises: the sizer now declines slots whose expected acceptance doesn't pay for their real cost.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py tests/v1/worker/test_mixed_warmup_gate.py` (25 passed). The budget and profiling tests were updated for the new model. A new test checks three things: the base charges the batch's actual context, each slot adds only its own price, and a budget crossing the capture limit picks up the graph-loss jump.
- [x] `pre-commit` hooks (ruff, mypy, and the rest) pass.
- [x] `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B` with DSpark adaptive verification starts, builds the base and slot tables, and serves chat requests.
- [x] Benchmarks above.

---

<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill. (Mandatory for agents, optional for humans).
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.

- [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.
</details>

items.title: [Sampling] Add adaptive verification support to batch-sharded sampling
items.body:
## Context
Batch-sharded sampling does not currently support adaptive verification: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/7e3d55956577605838e9babcba84dce354b0b78c/vllm/config/vllm.py#L3144-L3157

Batch sharding sizes its `all_to_all_single` splits and buffers from host-side per-request logit counts (`cu_num_logits_np`). Under adaptive verification, the per-request split of the draft budget is decided on device, so `cu_num_logits_np` only holds the scheduled counts (an upper bound), while the device `cu_num_logits` holds the admitted counts. Once the budget binds, the shard plan built on the host no longer matches the rows placed on device.

## This PR
When the draft budget binds, `reallocate_drafts` copies the per-request admitted draft counts to the host (async D2H on adaptive verification's copy stream). `shard_sampler_inputs` waits on that copy and builds the shard plan from the exact admitted counts, so the lm_head GEMM (`compute_logits_local`), the all-to-all, and the sampler run only on the rows that are actually verified. When the budget does not bind, the host counts are already exact and nothing is copied. The copy is only enabled when batch-sharded sampling is on (`copy_admitted_drafts_to_host`).

Also: the local draft count now follows the admitted budget, so with a budget of 0 every rank runs the same sampler as the replicated path.

### Tradeoff
The alternative is to keep the host's scheduled counts and pad each rank's segment up to them, which avoids any host wait but runs the GEMM, all-to-all, and sampler on the padded rows too. This PR instead adds a host wait in `sample()` on the admitted counts. It blocks the CPU only (the base model forward is already queued behind it), but it limits CPU run-ahead: the CPU cannot launch step N's sampling until the GPU has started step N. That costs ~0.05 ms per step at concurrency 1 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. The cost shrinks as the forward gets longer, so it matters least for large models at high concurrency, which are the cases batch-sharded sampling targets.

## Benchmarks

**Setup.** 4x GB200, TP4 + EP, vLLM `main` @ 7e3d559565 + this PR. `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark`, `--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","enable_adaptive_verification":true}'`, `--max-num-seqs 256 --max-model-len 32768 --block-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --moe-backend deep_gemm --enable-expert-parallel --no-enable-prefix-caching --kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune=False --compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size": 2048}'`. Both arms use adaptive verification; the sharded arm adds `--enable-batch-sharded-sampling`.

**Client.** `vllm-bench`, SPEED-Bench `throughput_2k` with placeholder prompts removed (905 prompts), max 2048 output tokens with natural EOS, temperature 1.0, `--num-warmups <conc>`, prompts = 8x concurrency (min 32, max 1024).

**Method.** Adaptive verification profiles its cost curves at every boot, and boot-to-boot differences in the curves moved median ITL by up to ~10% at some concurrencies, which swamped the effect. So the curves were saved from the first boot and loaded on every later boot (a benchmark-only patch, not part of this PR), and both arms make identical admission decisions. 4 boots in ABBA order, 2 sweeps per boot. One base boot was excluded for anomalously slow tail steps (−9 to −17% tok/s, with median ITL and acceptance normal), so n=2 for base and n=4 for sharded. Negative ITL/TPOT/TTFT is better.

| conc | tok/s base / shard | Δ | median ITL base / shard (ms) | Δ | median TPOT base / shard (ms) | Δ | mean TTFT Δ | accept len base / shard |
|---:|:---:|---:|:---:|---:|:---:|---:|---:|:---:|
| 1 | 330 / 332 | +0.5% | 9.34 / 9.39 | +0.59% | 2.68 / 2.72 | +1.5% | +0.1% | 3.22 / 3.25 |
| 4 | 960 / 964 | +0.4% | 11.43 / 11.43 | +0.09% | 3.70 / 3.66 | −1.1% | +3.3% | 3.21 / 3.17 |
| 8 | 1557 / 1550 | −0.4% | 13.20 / 13.17 | −0.19% | 4.67 / 4.61 | −1.3% | −0.6% | 3.13 / 3.13 |
| 16 | 2391 / 2405 | +0.6% | 15.15 / 15.10 | −0.31% | 6.08 / 6.08 | −0.2% | +3.2% | 3.12 / 3.14 |
| 32 | 3565 / 3536 | −0.8% | 17.15 / 17.10 | −0.31% | 8.53 / 8.40 | −1.5% | +2.3% | 3.04 / 3.03 |
| 64 | 4872 / 4874 | +0.0% | 19.97 / 19.81 | −0.78% | 12.28 / 12.35 | +0.6% | +1.3% | 2.92 / 2.93 |
| 128 | 6602 / 6558 | −0.7% | 25.09 / 24.80 | −1.12% | 18.34 / 18.55 | +1.1% | +2.2% | 2.84 / 2.84 |
| 256 | 9709 / 9676 | −0.3% | 32.17 / 31.78 | −1.21% | 24.48 / 24.66 | +0.8% | +3.7% | 2.71 / 2.71 |

**Result.** With the cost curves pinned, median ITL is consistent across boots (0.1–0.4% sd), and sharded sampling lowers it by 0.3–1.2% from concurrency 16 upward, growing with concurrency. At concurrency 1 it is +0.05 ms (+0.6%) on every run, which is the cost of the host wait. End-to-end throughput and TPOT are flat within run-to-run noise (tok/s sd 0.8–2.7%), because the median step improves while end-to-end time is dominated by slow prefill-heavy steps that sampling barely affects. Acceptance length matches at every concurrency.

I wasn't expecting to see an improvement in tok/s or TPOT, but rather to not regress it for the batch-sharded sampling cases. The main benefit of batch-sharded sampling is reducing the maximum target logits allocations by a factor of TP size from `B x (K + 1) x V => B x (K + 1) x V / P`.

### Block verification, top-p 0.95

Same setup and method as above, with `"rejection_sample_method":"block"` added to the speculative config and `--top-p 0.95` on the client, at concurrency 64-256. Cost curves pinned across boots; 4 boots in ABBA order, 2 sweeps per boot, n=4 per arm. Negative ITL/TPOT/TTFT is better.

| conc | tok/s base / shard | Δ | median ITL base / shard (ms) | Δ | median TPOT base / shard (ms) | Δ | mean TTFT Δ | accept len base / shard |
|---:|:---:|---:|:---:|---:|:---:|---:|---:|:---:|
| 64 | 4841 / 4810 | −0.6% | 20.42 / 20.07 | −1.7% | 12.37 / 12.38 | +0.1% | +1.0% | 2.96 / 2.97 |
| 128 | 6507 / 6501 | −0.1% | 25.84 / 25.18 | −2.6% | 18.54 / 18.62 | +0.5% | +3.1% | 2.89 / 2.89 |
| 256 | 9441 / 9569 | +1.4% | 32.91 / 32.02 | −2.7% | 25.08 / 24.71 | −1.5% | +2.8% | 2.72 / 2.72 |

Median ITL improves by 1.7-2.7%, about twice the gain with standard rejection sampling. Throughput and TPOT are flat at concurrency 64-128 (tok/s sd 0.7-2.5%) and improve at 256. Acceptance length matches at every concurrency. This optimization is more worthwhile when the sampling operations are more expensive.

## Testing
`pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_batch_shard.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py tests/v1/sample/test_dry.py`: 80 passed. Adds `test_admitted_counts_give_unpadded_plan`, which checks that an adaptive verification batch with copied admitted counts shards identically to a batch scheduled with only the admitted drafts.

items.title: [Core][CUDA Graph] Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes
items.body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

**Problem.** A CUDA graph replays a recorded step so the CPU does not launch each kernel. A batch with no graph of its size runs eagerly, and at serving batch sizes the CPU launching kernels, not the GPU, sets its speed. In model runner V2, one token list decides which batch sizes get graphs, for both prefill and decode. With speculative decoding each decode request carries 1 + K tokens, so a 1024-token list covers only 1024/(1+K) decode requests: 128 at K=7, while servers run up to 1024. On GB200, the models we validated spend 22–73% of engine time in such eager steps.

**Change.** Separate settings for prefill graphs, in tokens, and for decode graphs, in requests, each with its own cap. The old fields keep working, deprecated.
- Off SM100 the split keeps main's behavior, apart from the differences listed below.
- On SM100 (GB200/B200) each kind is sized on its own: decode graphs cover every batch size the scheduler can form, and prefill graphs reach 8192 tokens. That is where the speedup comes from.

This is the "separate prefill/decode graph sizes" item of the Q4 roadmap (#61024).

## Claims

On 4× GB200 with 256 concurrent requests:
- Throughput is ×1.3–3.2 of main on six MoE configurations and ×0.98–0.99 on a dense model.
- GSM8K answers match main within noise.
- KV cache is 0.63–0.98 of main. On DeepSeek most of the gap is today's memory estimate over-reserving; the rest is the sparse indexer's decode logits in the widest decode graph. See "KV cache on DeepSeek" under Differences from main; the fixes are listed in Follow-ups (memory estimate, a fair KV comparison, and the indexer logits).

## Configuration

### The four fields

They live on `CompilationConfig` (`--compilation-config '{...}'`) and come in two independent pairs.

| field | unit | what it controls | default on SM100 | default on other GPUs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens` | tokens | Cap: the largest prefill, chunked-prefill or mixed batch that runs as a CUDA graph (PIECEWISE). | `min(8192, max_num_batched_tokens)` | 512, as on main |
| `prefill_cudagraph_capture_token_sizes` | tokens | The exact token counts that get a prefill graph. Overrides the default grid. | 103 sizes up to 8192: main's grid up to 1024, then every 256 tokens up to 4096 and every 512 up to 8192 | main's list |
| `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests` | requests | Cap: the largest uniform decode batch, in requests, that runs as a FULL graph. | `max_num_seqs` (1024 with `vllm serve` on GB200) | main's request counts, 512 / (1 + K) |
| `decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes` | requests | The exact request counts that get a decode graph. Overrides the default grid. | every count up to 32, then 16 sizes per doubling (every 2 up to 64, every 4 up to 128, …): 112 sizes at 1024 | main's request counts |

**Graphs captured with the defaults.** GB200 `vllm serve`: `max_num_seqs` 1024, `max_num_batched_tokens` 16384, `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`. Each cell is the number of graphs, with the widest in parentheses.

| graphs | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| prefill, PIECEWISE | 83 (1024 tokens) | 103 (8192 tokens) |
| decode, FULL, no speculative decoding | 83 (1024 requests) | 112 (1024 requests) |
| EAGLE3 K=7: target decode, FULL | 80 (128 requests) | 112 (1024 requests) |
| EAGLE3 K=7: draft prefill, PIECEWISE / FULL | 83 / 80 | 103 / 112 |
| EAGLE3 K=7: one-token draft decode, FULL | 83 (1024 requests) | 112 (1024 requests) |
| DSpark K=7: target decode / DSpark, FULL | 80 (128) / 80 (144 requests) | 112 (1024) / 112 (1024 requests) |

**Memory per kind.** Each kind of graph costs memory in two places:
- **Graph objects:** the driver's memory for each instantiated graph (`cudaGraphExec`), outside the torch allocator. There is one per graph, so it grows with the count: 15–18 MiB per PIECEWISE size, 10–18 MiB per target FULL graph, 0.4–1.2 MiB per drafter graph. Capture takes 1–1.5 s per PIECEWISE size (two passes), 0.5 s per target FULL graph and 10–50 ms per drafter graph.
- **Its widest graph's tensors, in the graph pool.** All graphs share one private pool of the torch allocator, which holds the tensors their kernels pass to each other. Graphs are captured widest first and the narrower ones reuse the freed blocks. So a kind needs the pool only as large as its widest graph, and the pool is the largest of these needs, not their sum.

Measured per GPU on rank 0 (rank 3 agrees within 2 MiB), main and this PR on one node, the 60a7d568f4 wheel, the PR validation's serve commands. DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DSpark K=7, TP4+EP, is the largest case:

| GiB | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| **target prefill, PIECEWISE** | 83 graphs, up to 1024 tokens | 103 graphs, up to 8192 tokens |
| ↳ graph objects | 1.60 | 2.01 |
| ↳ widest graph's tensors | 0.19 | 1.55 |
| **target decode, FULL** | 80 graphs, up to 128 requests × 8 tokens | 112 graphs, up to 1024 requests × 8 tokens |
| ↳ graph objects | 1.33 | 1.79 |
| ↳ widest graph's tensors | 1.70 | 13.58 |
| ↳ of which the sparse indexer's decode logits | 1.50 | 12.02 |
| **DSpark draft decode, FULL** | 80 graphs, up to 144 requests | 112 graphs, up to 1024 requests |
| ↳ graph objects | 0.06 | 0.10 |
| ↳ widest graph's tensors | 0.57 | 4.05 |
| **graph pool, all streams** | 4.33 | 22.11 |
| ↳ of which aux hidden states kept by every PIECEWISE size (below) | 0.82 | 2.74 |
| ↳ of which DSpark's own capture stream (below) | 0.74 | 5.23 |
| default pool and other memory added by capture | 0.29 | 1.18 |
| **the real capture** (the log's `actual`) | **5.81** | **24.79** |
| **all graph memory at rest**, with the PIECEWISE objects | **8.0** | **27.4** |

- The parts overlap inside the pool (a graph reuses blocks freed by wider ones), so they do not add up to the totals; each total is measured.
- The PIECEWISE objects are allocated in the profiling pass and kept for the process lifetime, so the log's `actual` leaves them out.
- A pool can reserve more than its widest graph needs: main's widest decode graph needs 1.70 GiB but reserves 2.67, because its FP32 indexer logits took a second segment through fragmentation.
- This PR's "default pool and other" is mostly persistent output buffers sized for 8192 tokens (0.25 against 0.03 GiB) and free space pinned in their segments.
- **The decode width is the one large cost, and only DeepSeek pays it:** its widest decode graph holds the sparse indexer's decode logits, `max_model_len` / 4 × 6 B per token. To give memory back, lower `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests` (see "How to use them"). Sharing one logits buffer between graphs and eager steps is listed under Follow-ups.
- **With both changes below,** this PR's pool measures 14.1 GiB: the PIECEWISE graphs and DSpark's fit inside the widest decode graph. A prefill-only instance's pool measures 2.1 GiB.
- **MiniMax-M3, EAGLE3 K=3, TP4** (main → this PR, GiB): PIECEWISE objects 1.38 → 1.93; target and EAGLE3 FULL objects 0.91 → 1.31; graph pool 1.80 → 5.84, of which aux hidden states 1.22 → 4.09 and EAGLE3's own capture streams 0.30 → 0.85; the real capture 3.15 → 8.13; all graph memory at rest 4.6 → 10.2. With both changes, this PR's whole pool is its widest PIECEWISE graph, 1.9 GiB.
- **Off SM100** (H100/H200 defaults), prefill and target decode keep main's 51 / 51 graphs. Only the one-token draft decodes grow, from 51 to 112.

With an EAGLE3, DSpark or DFlash drafter, two more behaviors add memory. Both exist on main too. The first grows with the captured PIECEWISE tokens and the second with the drafter's widest graph, so both cost more on this PR:
- **Every PIECEWISE size keeps its own aux hidden states.**
  - These drafters read three of the target's intermediate hidden states. The target's PIECEWISE graph returns them as `(hidden_states, [aux, ...])`.
  - After each capture, the graph wrapper turns its output into weak references, so that the next size can reuse the output's memory in the pool. `weak_ref_tensors` converts only the outer tuple, so the inner list stays a strong reference.
  - Each captured size then holds 3 × tokens × hidden × 2 B for the life of the engine: 192 MiB at 8192 tokens on DeepSeek-V4. The total grows with the sum of all captured PIECEWISE tokens, not with the widest.
  - Keeping a copy per size does not look necessary. The drafter copies the aux states right after the target's replay, before any other graph replays, and the `hidden_states` output, already weak, relies on the same order. Letting `weak_ref_tensors` recurse frees them (https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb), with the same GSM8K answers and acceptance on DeepSeek-V4 and M3.
- **Drafter graphs cannot reuse the target's free memory in the pool.**
  - The target and each drafter capture through their own `CudaGraphManager.capture()`, and each call opens a new CUDA stream (`graph_capture()`). They all capture into the same pool.
  - The caching allocator hands a free block only to requests on the stream that allocated it. So the drafter's widest graph reserves new memory for its whole peak, even when the pool has enough free, and its narrower graphs reuse that. In effect the drafter gets its own share of the pool.
  - On DeepSeek-V4 DSpark K=7, DSpark's widest graph reserved 5.35 GiB while the pool held 14.2 GiB free. On M3, EAGLE3's graphs add 0.84 GiB.
  - #59537 (open) captures with one stream per device; then DSpark's graphs fit inside the target's pool. It should land with the aux-state change: without that change and without NUMA binding, it slowed breakable PIECEWISE steps 1.2–1.6× in 4 of 4 launches, cause open.

**Rules.**
- A cap alone captures the default grid up to the cap. A list alone captures exactly those sizes; sizes above `max_num_batched_tokens` (prefill) or `max_num_seqs` (decode) are dropped with a warning.
- With both a list and its cap, the list's max must not exceed the cap. A follow-up will require them to match, as main does for the old pair.
- `[]` captures none of that kind. Both `[]` turns CUDA graphs off.
- The pairs are independent: setting one never changes the other's graphs.
- Under `cudagraph_mode` FULL or PIECEWISE, which do not separate decode batches, every batch uses the prefill sizes.

### How to use them

The defaults suit most deployments. Change a cap when one of these applies:

```bash
# KV cache is short, e.g. DeepSeek-V4 at long context: decode graphs up to 512 requests.
# Prefill graphs are unchanged. Measured: about 6 GiB back, 5-11% slower at 1024 concurrent requests.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests": 512}'

# MoE model at DP = 1 with 8K+ prompts: prefill graphs up to 16K tokens (needs max_num_batched_tokens >= 16384).
# Measured: up to 25% less engine time. With EAGLE3 or DSpark drafters it costs 2-8 GiB more while every PIECEWISE size keeps its own aux hidden states.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 16384}'

# Dense model at small TP: graphs above about 1.5K tokens neither help nor hurt there; this saves startup time.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 2048}'

# Prefill instance in a prefill/decode disaggregated deployment: it runs no decode batches.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes": []}'
```

The default grids are tuned: the decode grid pads by at most 0.6% of target time, and the prefill grid by about 1%. An exact list replaces them, so set one only for batch sizes you know the deployment runs. A sparse list pads: a power-of-two decode list loses 3–4.5% of engine time against the default grid.

### With speculative decoding

A decode size is a request count. Each runner turns it into tokens with its own query length `q`:

| runner | `q` | graph for `decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes=[64]` at K = 7 |
|---|---|---|
| target | 1 + K | 512 tokens |
| EAGLE / EAGLE3 / MTP draft steps after the first | 1 | 64 tokens |
| DSpark | K | 448 tokens |
| DFlash, multi-module MTP | K + 1 | 512 tokens |

- **Decode coverage no longer shrinks as K grows.** The graph's width does grow: 1024 requests at K = 7 is an 8192-token graph.
- **One-token draft steps always cover `max_num_seqs`**, even when the target's decode cap is lower; only `[]` turns them off. Each of their K − 1 eager steps would otherwise pay its host launches.
- **Multi-token drafters (DSpark, DFlash, multi-module MTP) follow the target's decode sizes.** Extending them waits for #59537, which lets their graphs share the target's memory pool.
- **Dynamic speculative decoding** (`num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size`): each tier gets the request counts its schedule reaches, at its own `q`.

### With adaptive verification

Adaptive-verification decode batches mix query lengths, so they take token-keyed FULL graphs on the prefill grid. These go up to `min(max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests × (1 + K), max_num_batched_tokens)` tokens: lowering the decode cap also narrows them. On DeepSeek-V4.1 (K = 5, 1024 requests) the widest is 6144 tokens.

### Migrating from the old fields

**Nothing breaks.** `cudagraph_capture_sizes` and `max_cudagraph_capture_size` still work on model runner V2 and capture what they captured on main, with a deprecation warning. Only mixing old and new fields in one config is an error. Model runner V1 is unchanged.

**To switch,** delete the old field and the defaults above apply. To set the caps yourself, give each kind its own value: prefill in tokens, decode in requests.

```bash
# Before: one cap for both kinds, in tokens.
--compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size": 1024}'

# After: prefill graphs up to 1024 tokens, and a decode graph for every batch up to max_num_seqs (here 1024).
--compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 1024, "max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests": 1024}'
```

## Why this design

**Why not just raise the cap on main.** One list serves both kinds, so covering decode drags prefill along at main's fine spacing.
- At K=7, `max_cudagraph_capture_size=8192` makes main capture 531 PIECEWISE sizes (one every 16 tokens above 256) and 528 FULL decode graphs for 1024 sequences.
- At the per-graph costs measured here, that is about 16–18 GiB of graph-exec memory and 12–18 minutes of capture (estimated, not run).
- The right cap also moves with K: 8192 tokens is 1024 requests at K=7 but 512 at K=15.

This PR covers the same range with 103 PIECEWISE and 112 FULL decode graphs.

**Prefill cap: 8192.** Measured on the MoE models this PR targets. Engine time is for 8K-token prompts with 1K output tokens at 16 concurrent requests, with the 16K cap = 1.00 (lower is faster). PIECEWISE graph memory is per GPU, as of today.

| model, parallelism | prefill graphs pay off up to | engine time at cap 8K / 12K / 16K | PIECEWISE graph memory at 8K / 12K / 16K |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4+EP | 15–16K tokens | 1.33 / 1.00 / 1.00 | 3.0 / 5.0 / 7.7 GiB |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, TP4+EP | ~16.5K | 1.13 / 1.02 / 1.00 | 3.2 / 5.8 / 6.4 GiB |
| MiniMax-M3, TP4 | 12.5–13.8K | 1.20 / 0.99 / 1.00 | 4.8 / 8.0 / 12.4 GiB |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DP4+EP | ~9K | 1.14 / 1.02 / 1.00 | 3.6 / 6.5 / 9.4 GiB |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DP4+EP | – | **0.86** / 1.00 / 1.00 | 8.4 / 12.3 / 16.2 GiB |

Why 8192:
- **Every MoE model keeps gaining from prefill graphs well past main's 1024-token cap** (9–16.5K tokens), so the cap must go up.
- **8192 is the largest cap that gains on every config measured and regresses none.** Two problems make 12K and 16K a trade today:
  - PIECEWISE graph memory grows with the cap: 8K → 16K adds 4.7 GiB on DeepSeek-V4 TP4+EP and 7.6 GiB on M3, because every PIECEWISE size keeps its own aux hidden states (see "Where the memory goes"; main does the same).
    - Freeing them (https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb) brings the increase down to +2.0 and +1.3 GiB.
  - With DP > 1 and a gather-based MoE path (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next DP4+EP), any cap above 8K is 14–20% slower, because each rank computes the other ranks' padded rows. That needs the gather-based MoE to skip padded rows, which no open PR does.
- **Next step:** once the aux-state change lands, raise the default to 16K at DP = 1, for up to 25% less engine time on long prompts. Keep 8192 at DP > 1 until the gather-based MoE skips padded rows.
- A dense model is not the target. A dense 27B at TP1 stops gaining at about 1.5K, and larger graphs neither help nor hurt it, so the default is harmless there.

**Decode cap: `max_num_seqs`.** Main divides its 1024-token list by 1 + K, so the share of decode batch sizes that get a graph falls as K grows. This PR covers every batch size the scheduler can form, at any K.

![Decode FULL graph hit rate: this PR hits a graph at every batch size up to max_num_seqs at any K; main stops at 1024 / (1 + K) requests](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pb314314/vllm/cg-pr-assets/decode_full_graph_hit_rate.png)

| K | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main: largest decode batch with a graph | 512 | 341 | 256 | 170 | 128 |
| this PR | 1024 | 1024 | 1024 | 1024 | 1024 |

Decode steps are launch-bound at every batch size, so every batch should get a graph. The cost is the widest graph's memory; see "How to use them".

The table of all defaults and the measurements behind them, including the choice of decode grid, are under Details.

**Commits.**
1. Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes.
2. Default to wider CUDA graphs on SM100.
3. One-token draft decode graphs cover `max_num_seqs`.
4. Disable CUDA graphs when no capture size is left.
5. Bound decode graphs by the recorded max capture size.
6. Keep GPT-OSS's decode coverage under dynamic speculative decoding.
7. Bound KDA recoverSSM mixed graphs by 1 + K tokens per request.

**Gains**
- **SM100 defaults.**

### Motivation: what a CUDA graph buys, what it costs

**What it buys: host launch time.** An eager step costs roughly max(host launch time, GPU time). A graph replay removes almost all of the host part.
- **Decode steps** are launch-bound at serving batch sizes, so a FULL decode graph always pays off. On Qwen3-8B EAGLE3 K=7, the six draft steps of one decode step take 6.2–7.0 ms of host time eagerly, against 0.17 ms for one replay (measured on builds with per-step tracing).
- **Prefill and mixed steps** are launch-bound only up to a crossover size, s* ≈ T_launch / g, where g is the GPU time per token per rank. Past s* the GPU work hides the launches, and a PIECEWISE graph gains nothing.
  - Measured on GB200: about 15–16K tokens on DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP4+EP, about 16.5K on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next TP4+EP, 12.5–13.8K on MiniMax-M3 TP4, and about 1.5K on a dense 27B model at TP1.
  - So the useful prefill cap depends on the model, the hardware and the parallelism, not on the decode width.

**What it costs**, per graph kind:
- **Graph-pool memory comes from the widest graph, not the number of graphs.** Every graph of a process is captured into one shared pool, and later graphs reuse the blocks earlier graphs freed.
- **The number of graphs costs graph-exec memory and startup time:**
  - each PIECEWISE size: 15–18 MiB, and 0.45–0.74 s in each of the two capture passes;
  - each target FULL graph: about 16 MiB and 0.5 s;
  - each drafter graph: 0.5–1.2 MiB and 10–50 ms.

So graph count is cheap, and graph width is what has to be weighed.

**Why one list does not work.** The token list mixes two different quantities:
- **It sizes prefill graphs in tokens**, which is the right unit for them.
- **It caps decode graphs at `T / (1 + K)` requests**, where K is the number of speculative tokens. The decode coverage therefore shrinks as K grows. Each runner also rounds the list to its own query length.
- **Raising one kind's coverage raises the other's.** Getting decode graphs to 1024 requests at K=7 needs an 8192-token cap. On main that cap also means 531 PIECEWISE sizes at its fine spacing (see Overview).
- **On GB200 with main, the models we validated spend 22–73% of engine time in eager steps.** Those steps are mixed steps above the 1024-token cap and decode batches above 1024/(1+K) requests.

### Prefill graphs (tokens)

- **What is captured.** Token-keyed graphs, PIECEWISE under `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`.
- **Default on SM100 (commit 2).** Up to `min(8192, max_num_batched_tokens)` tokens.
  - The grid is main's up to 1024 tokens (1, 2, 4, then steps of 8 up to 256 and steps of 16), then steps of 256 up to 4096, then steps of 512.
  - With `vllm serve` defaults on GB200 that is 103 graphs, against main's 83 up to 1024.
- **Default on other GPUs, and with the deprecated fields.** Main's list, 51 graphs up to 512 tokens.
- **Why 8192.** It is below every measured s* except the dense TP1 model's. On that model, prefill graphs above s* neither help nor hurt (engine time 0.996–0.998 of the 16K cap).
  - 16K would be better for single-DP MoE models on 8K-prompt workloads, by 13–33%. An 8K chunk plus the decodes that ride along lands just above 8192, so at 8192 it runs eagerly. A replicate with two server instances per cap on DeepSeek-V4-Flash TEP, 8K/1K at concurrency 16, gives 8192 / 16384 engine time 1.357 (sd 0.032, n = 12).
  - 16K waits for two changes listed under Follow-ups (T4, T5). The first frees the aux hidden states every PIECEWISE size keeps. The second is the gather-based DP/EP MoE path, which computes padded rows under DP > 1.
- **Why this grid.** Steps of 256 and 512 above 1024 keep padding near 1% on the TP4 MoE models. Halving the steps gains 0.3–0.4% and costs 28 more graphs.
- **Cost.**
  - The 20 extra graphs add about 20–30 s of startup and 0.3–0.4 GiB of graph-exec memory.
  - The pool holds the widest graph's peak: 2.06 GiB on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 1.88 GiB on M3 at 8192 tokens.
  - Today memory also grows per size: every breakable PIECEWISE size keeps the drafter's aux hidden states. That is +2.72 GiB on DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark and +4.09 GiB on M3 EAGLE3 with this grid, against +0.81 / +1.21 GiB with main's grid. Freeing them is a separate PR (T4).

### Decode graphs (requests)

- **What is captured.** FULL graphs for uniform decode batches, keyed by request count. Each runner uses its own query length:
  - the target: `q = 1 + K`;
  - one-token draft decodes: `q = 1`;
  - DSpark: `q = K`;
  - DFlash and multi-module MTP: `q = K + 1`.
- **Default on SM100 (commit 2).** Up to `max_num_seqs` requests at any K. The grid has every count up to 32, then 16 sizes per doubling (every 2 up to 64, every 4 up to 128, …). That is 112 graphs at `max_num_seqs` 1024.
  - Main covers 1024/(1+K) requests: 128 at K=7, 256 at K=3.
- **Default on other GPUs, and with the deprecated fields.** Main's request counts: what main's token list holds at the target's `q`. At K=7 that is 48 graphs up to 64 requests.
- **Why up to `max_num_seqs`.** Then every decode batch the scheduler can form has a FULL graph.
  - The cost is width. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DSpark K=7, 1K/1K, concurrency 1024, equal KV, three launches per arm), capping at 512 instead of 1024 requests saves 6.0 GiB per GPU and costs about 5% throughput (11% counting a third launch that ran slow throughout, cause open). All of that is the DSpark drafter's eager fallback: with the target at 512 and DSpark at 1024, throughput equals 1024 / 1024 (0.999).
  - Decode-only steps above the cap run PIECEWISE, about 7% slower each. On a decode-heavy 1K/4K concurrency 1024 the cap at 512 costs nothing measurable (0.986, two launches per arm). The 1K/1K cost comes from host-bound mixed steps.
  - Users who need the KV can lower `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests`.
- **Why this grid.** Padded rows are not free.
  - A padded row costs 0.56–0.78 of a real row on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 0.90–0.93 on M3, and 1.44–1.65 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
  - Per operator (in-graph timing and kernel profiles), a padded row costs what a real one does in GEMMs past the ~280-row compute ridge (`q × n` rows, 384 at K=3 and 96 requests), norms and collectives; attention skips it.
  - Routed experts skip it only where the MoE reads `is_padding` (DeepSeek-V4's mega-MoE). The TRT-LLM monolithic MoE on M3 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next computes padded tokens.
  - On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 63% of the padded cost is one sparse-indexer kernel at ~87 µs per padded request: DeepGEMM's SM schedule puts every padded row on the last SM. Scheduling only the real rows, a separate fix outside this PR, brings DeepSeek-V4's padded/real cost from 1.44–1.51 to 0.54–0.57 (measured).
  - Under serving batch distributions this grid pads at most 0.6% of target time.
  - Denser grids (every count up to 64 then 32 per doubling, or every count) gain at most 0.3% end to end. Power-of-two grids lose 3–4.5% of engine time (3.0–6.5% tok/s).
- **Cost.**
  - Count: 112 target graphs take about 1.8 GiB of graph-exec memory and about 1 min of capture.
  - Width: the widest graph has `max_num_seqs × q` tokens. It costs about 0.8 GiB on M3 (K=3).
  - On DeepSeek-V4-Flash (K=7, 8192 tokens) it costs about 14 GiB. About 12 GiB of that is the sparse indexer's decode logits, which scale with `max_model_len`: 8192 rows × 262144 × 6 B at 1M context. See Differences from main.

### Adaptive verification

- **What is captured.** Decode batches mix query lengths under adaptive verification. They take token-keyed FULL graphs on the prefill grid up to `min(max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests × (1 + K), max_num_batched_tokens)` tokens. At K=5 on SM100 that is 99 graphs up to 6144 tokens, against main's 85 up to 1024.
- **Why it shares the prefill grid.**
  - Adaptive verification trims its budget to a captured size, so its decode steps pad at most 0.24%.
  - Six grids × 5 workloads × 3 seeds all came within ±2% of each other.
  - A grid that differs from the prefill grid pads the mixed steps by 7–10%, and mixed steps are 15–92% of its steps.
- **Cost.** 11.2 MiB and 0.64 s per graph. The pool is set by the widest graph: on DeepSeek-V4.1 with 1024 × 6 tokens, about 12 GiB more than main.

### Drafter graphs

- **Draft prefill** (EAGLE, EAGLE3 and MTP draft position 0) runs the target's batch shape. It has the same graphs as the target: PIECEWISE plus FULL at `q = K + 1`.
- **One-token draft decodes** are the EAGLE, EAGLE3 and MTP draft steps after the first. After commit 3 they use the decode request counts, extended past their widest by the decode grid up to `max_num_seqs`.
  - This holds on every GPU and however the decode sizes are set. `[]` still captures none.
  - Why: a draft graph is cheap (0.5–1.2 MiB and 10–50 ms; the widest holds the drafter's logits, see Differences from main), but eager draft steps pay their host launches on every step. On Qwen3-8B EAGLE3 K=7 that is +6 ms per decode step, and +11–15 ms on M3 (builds with per-step tracing). On plain builds, commits 1–2 run 15% / 9% / 3.5% below the head at concurrency 128 / concurrency 256 / concurrency 512, and commit 3 closes that gap (Validation).
  - Without commit 3 these graphs stopped at the target's cap: 64 requests off SM100 at K=7, where main covered 512.
- **Multi-token drafters** (DSpark, DFlash, multi-module MTP) run one forward of `q = K` or `K + 1` tokens per request, on the target's request counts.
  - On SM100 they reach `max_num_seqs`; main stopped at 144 requests for DSpark K=7. Off SM100, DSpark (q = K) now stops at the target's cap, K/(K+1) of main's coverage (see Differences from main); DFlash and multi-module MTP match main.
  - Their graphs never exceed the recorded `max_cudagraph_capture_size`, as on main, also under dynamic SD.
  - Extending them past the target's cap waits for #59537. Today each graph manager captures on its own CUDA stream, and the caching allocator does not reuse blocks across streams.
  - So DSpark's widest graph takes its own memory: 5.35 GiB at 1024 requests on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. With #59537 it fits in the target's free pool, for +20 MiB (measured).
  - On DeepSeek-V4-Flash at concurrency 1024 with the target capped at 512, extending the DSpark graphs from 512 to 1024 requests gains about 5–11% (three launches per arm) and reaches the 1024 / 1024 throughput at an 8.11 GiB pool instead of 14.11 GiB, with #59537.

### Graphs per kind, main vs this PR

CPU capture plans with `vllm serve` defaults: GB200 has `max_num_seqs` 1024 and `max_num_batched_tokens` 16384; H100/H200 have 1024 and 8192. `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`. Each cell is the number of graphs, with the widest in parentheses.

| config | graphs | GB200 main | GB200 PR | H100/H200 main | H100/H200 PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no SD | target PIECEWISE (tokens) | 83 (1024) | 103 (8192) | 51 (512) | 51 (512) |
| | target FULL decode (requests) | 83 (1024) | 112 (1024) | 51 (512) | 51 (512) |
| EAGLE3 K=7 | target PIECEWISE (tokens) | 83 (1024) | 103 (8192) | 51 (512) | 51 (512) |
| | target FULL decode (requests) | 80 (128) | 112 (1024) | 48 (64) | 48 (64) |
| | draft prefill PIECEWISE / FULL | 83 / 80 | 103 / 112 | 51 / 48 | 51 / 48 |
| | one-token draft decode FULL (requests) | 83 (1024) | 112 (1024) | 51 (512) | **112 (1024)** |
| EAGLE3 K=3 | target FULL decode (requests) | 81 (256) | 112 (1024) | 49 (128) | 49 (128) |
| | one-token draft decode FULL (requests) | 83 (1024) | 112 (1024) | 51 (512) | 97 (1024) |
| DSpark K=7 | target FULL decode (requests) | 80 (128) | 112 (1024) | 48 (64) | 48 (64) |
| | DSpark FULL (requests, q = K) | 80 (144) | 112 (1024) | 48 (71) | **48 (64)** |
| DSpark K=5 + AV | target AV FULL (tokens) | 85 (1024) | 99 (6144) | 53 (512) | **51 (498)** |
| | DSpark FULL (requests, q = K) | 81 (202) | 112 (1024) | 49 (100) | **48 (83)** |

The bold cells off SM100 are the differences from main. Each one is explained under Differences from main. The recorded `max_cudagraph_capture_size` follows the widest graph: on GB200 it is 8192 (main: 1024). Off SM100 with a one-token drafter it is `max_num_seqs` (main: 512).

</details>

## Follow-ups

- [ ] **T1. A size list and its cap must agree**, as main requires for the legacy pair. Raise when both are set and the cap differs from the list's max. Today a decode cap above the list's max is silently lowered, so adaptive verification follows the list while the docstring says it follows the cap. *Small; the next version of this PR.*
- [ ] **T2. Minimality cuts.** About 56 lines of docstrings and comments, and 25–30 lines of code, can go without changing behavior. A reviewer's list is ready. *Small; the next version of this PR.*
- [ ] **T3. Multi-token drafters (DSpark, DFlash, multi-module MTP) cover `max_num_seqs`**, with their shapes recorded in the max. *Depends on #59537 (one capture stream per device, aoshen02, draft).*
  - Without #59537, the widest draft graph needs its own memory: 2.7 GiB more at 1024 than at 512 requests on DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
  - Gain: 5–11% at DeepSeek-V4-Flash concurrency 1024 with the target at 512.
- [ ] **T4. Free the aux hidden states each PIECEWISE size keeps.** The change is ready on a branch, not yet proposed upstream: https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb. Breakable PIECEWISE graphs keep the drafter's aux hidden states alive per size, because `weak_ref_tensors` goes one level deep.
  - It costs 2.7–8 GiB on DeepSeek-V4, M3 and Kimi-K3.
  - The change is 12 lines plus a test, and gives KV +3.9% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and +4.4% on M3. *Separate PR; also on main.*
- [ ] **T5. Prefill cap 16K at DP = 1**, after T4. 8192 / 16384 engine time is 1.357 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash TEP 8K/1K. Under DP > 1 it stays 8192 until the gather-based DP/EP MoE skips padded rows: on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next DP4+EP, 8K is 14–20% faster.
- [ ] **T6. The CUDA graph memory estimate.**
  - Fix order: #59368 without its double count with #60186, then #62860, #61509, #57926 and #59537, then budgets for our persistent output buffers and for M3's and Kimi's workspaces.
  - Each fix is measured on its own. The combined stack has not run.
  - Most of this PR's DeepSeek KV gap comes from the estimate: see Differences from main.
- [ ] **T7. DeepSeek-V4 sparse-indexer padding.** DeepGEMM's SM schedule runs every padded decode row on the last SM.
  - Building the schedule over the real rows brings the padded/real cost from 1.44–1.51 to 0.54–0.57, with the same GSM8K. End to end it is −1 to −3% TPOT with this PR's decode grid.
  - *Separate PR.*
- [ ] **T8. A drafter cap separate from the target's.** The widest one-token draft graph holds the drafter's logits: +1.02 GiB for Gemma 4 E2B's 262k vocabulary.
- [ ] **T9. DSpark's request counts from its own q**, closing the K/(K+1) window off SM100. At concurrency 68 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash K=7 that window measured −4% / −10% (n = 2, not resolved).
- [ ] **T10. Open checks.**
  - DeepSeek-V4.1's decoder-replay bound follows the widest graph: about 32 replay sizes on GB200 against 8, roughly 0.5 GiB. This is estimated from code; measure it on GB200.
  - DeepSeek-V4.1's specialized-decode `metadata_graphs.capture_keys` still bounds its keys by `max_num_batched_tokens`. Under dynamic SD it can record keys that never run. GB300 only.
  - Dynamic-SD tiers capture only the request counts their schedule reaches. A uniform batch formed outside its tier would run PIECEWISE, where main ran FULL. Check with a scheduler trace under token-budget pressure.
- [ ] **T11. Coverage this cluster cannot run.**
  - H100/H200: off-SM100 graph sets were only emulated on GB200.
  - DFlash and multi-module MTP on GPU: no cached model pair.
  - Prefill context parallel, multi-node TP and LoRA end to end.
- [ ] **T12. Measure main with `max_cudagraph_capture_size=8192`** end to end, to replace the Overview's estimate of its graph cost.
- [ ] **T13. A fair KV comparison on DeepSeek.** Apply the estimate fixes to both main and this PR (#59368, #61509, #62860, and #60186 without its double count), then compare KV on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Expected, derived: V4.1 at or above main; V4 at about 0.85–0.9 of main, and about 1.0 with T14.
- [ ] **T14. DeepSeek's sparse-indexer decode logits.** Share one logits buffer between the decode graphs and the eager path, or compute the logits in request chunks on SM100, as #62169 does on SM90/SM120. That removes about 10 GiB per GPU at 1024 requests × 8 tokens. A separate PR.

## Not a duplicate

- #61882 refactors decode/mixed planning without a config change.
- #62209 adds an opt-in prefill subset of the shared list.
- #56136 and #62040 patch dynamic-SD and DSpark reachability. This PR covers both by construction, and their cases are in the tests.
- #60265 changes the default floor.
- None of them separates the two kinds' units and caps.

items.title: [Spec Decode] Expose adaptive verified draft token count
items.body:
## Purpose

Expose the actual draft-token verification budget when adaptive verification is enabled. The existing draft counter counts proposals, which may be longer than the prefix sent to the target verifier.

This PR adds:

- `vllm:spec_decode_num_verified_draft_tokens_total` and the verified count in server logs.
- `vllm:spec_decode_num_verified_draft_tokens_per_pos_total{position="..."}`, with zero-based positions. A verified prefix of length 3 increments positions 0, 1, and 2; the sum across positions equals the scalar verified count.
- Documentation and unit tests for verified-token accounting.

Both verified counters are exposed only with adaptive verification enabled. They exclude bonus tokens and use the same request filtering as proposal accounting, including excluding results for already-finished requests. With async scheduling and structured outputs, grammar-invalid positions can still be physically verified, so verified counts can exceed grammar-adjusted proposal counts.

MRV2 reports per-request verified lengths through the async output-copy path. The per-position extension reuses the same CPU integers as the scalar counter, adding no further GPU kernel, D2H copy, or synchronization. It adds up to K CPU list increments per observed request, a K-entry stats vector, and K counter updates per observed batch. Overhead has not been benchmarked.

This extends the existing verified-token accounting in this PR. Related #54748 records the scheduler-selected K, including no-draft steps; it measures a different stage from the verifier's actual admitted prefix.

## Validation

CPU-only tests ran from this PR's full Python source on Linux/Python 3.12.3 with PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130 and native artifacts reused from the existing vLLM 0.32.1rc1.dev183+g7e3d55956 environment. No GPU serving or model evaluation was run for the appended CPU counter change.

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/metrics/test_stats.py -v
```

```text
============================== 21 passed in 2.41s ==============================
```

Using a local Hugging Face cache containing OPT-125M config/tokenizer files:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 \
  HF_HUB_CACHE=/opt/pr58340_per_position_20261022/hf-cache OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
    -k "spec_decoding_stats or adaptive_verification_stats_count_actual_budget" -v
```

```text
====================== 11 passed, 196 deselected in 4.34s ======================
```

Coverage includes different prefix distributions with the same verified total, zero/missing verified counts, AV-disabled metric gating, stats serialization, grammar-invalid positions, and finished-request filtering. The new position assertions fail on the preceding commit because the per-position verified field is absent.

```bash

```

items.title: [Core] Add defer mode for long prefills
items.body:
## Purpose

Adds `--long-prefill-token-threshold-defer`, off by default. Instead of capping each long prefill at `long_prefill_token_threshold`, long prefills take turns:
- one long prefill per step;
- it runs after the waiting requests, with the leftover budget, if that is at least the threshold;
- one that sat out its turn runs first the next step.

**Why:** with context parallelism, each step costs a fixed amount, plus an amount for each request in it that grows with its context. On H200 (GLM-5.3, PCP8×DCP8, 8192 tokens per step) that is about 230 ms fixed, plus about 335 ms for a request at 1M context. Splitting the budget pays these costs more often. Under load the adaptive threshold also splits short cached prompts, which cuts throughput just when the queue is longest.

## Results

Agent X ([Weka trace](https://huggingface.co/datasets/semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126)) with GLM-5.3 at 1M context on 16× H200: PCP8/DCP8 prefill → DP8 decode. This commit on an earlier main, all arms in one run, 20 minutes per point. Adaptive = threshold 2048 + adaptive; defer = threshold 2048 + defer.

| concurrency | arm | requests | TTFT p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | adaptive | 1186 | 1.3 s | 7.2 s | 105 s |
| 32 | no threshold | 1205 | 1.3 s | 7.7 s | 44 s |
| 32 | defer | 1176 | 1.4 s | 29.9 s | 66 s |
| 48 | adaptive | 464 | 1.7 s | 510 s | 559 s |
| 48 | no threshold | 762 | 2.6 s | 276 s | 326 s |
| 48 | **defer** | 744 | 3.7 s | **198 s** | **264 s** |

- **Under load (concurrency 48):** defer completes 60% more requests than adaptive, matches no threshold on throughput, and has the best tail.
- **Concurrency 32:** within run-to-run noise. A repeat of defer reached 1227 requests with p95 6.5 s, the best of all c32 runs. Variants that ran long prefills oldest-first or one at a time were worse (p95 32–35 s): medium prompts got stuck behind the largest one.
- **Noise:** the same arm varies by up to ±24% in requests between runs at concurrency 48.
- **Accuracy:** gsm8k is the same in all arms (0.728–0.740).

## Test plan

`pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -k long_prefill`

items.title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Align adaptive draft prefill graph padding
items.body:
## Overview

Fixes #62793. Align target-dependent draft-prefill CUDA graph padding with the target's shared attention metadata when adaptive verification is enabled.

## Claims

- Capture varlen draft-prefill graphs under AV and pass a decode-only query-length bound at dispatch.
- Keep AV-disabled decode and prefill-bearing fallback behavior covered by regression tests.

## Validation

Current base: `c2861f7f120d508dcb1be046d9fc659c93062508`.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/v1/cudagraph \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py \
  -k draft_prefill_matches_shared_target_metadata_shape -q
```

Before the fix: **2 failed, 2 passed, 23 deselected**. The AV cases expose mismatched request padding and a PIECEWISE fallback instead of the target's FULL graph.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/v1/cudagraph \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py \
  -k 'not test_full_capture_sets_graph_pool_id_before_cuda_graph' -q
```

After the fix: **26 passed, 1 deselected**. Running the whole file on this macOS host produced 26 passes and one failure in the existing graph-pool capture test: the unspecified platform cannot create a current stream. The command above excludes that platform-dependent test; CUDA CI is still needed.

```bash
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/target_dependent_ar/speculator.py \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py
git diff --check
```

All applicable hooks passed, including Ruff, mypy and test tethering; `git diff --check` passed.

The equivalent candidate-source fix was previously validated end to end on **v0.31.0**, H100 NVL, Qwen3-32B W4A16 + Eagle3, K=3, FA3, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, concurrency 4, with 10s warmup and 30s measurement per run:

| Configuration | Output tok/s, mean (two independent starts) | Range | Mean acceptance length |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Unpatched AV | 352.4 | 351.5–353.3 | 1.425 |
| Candidate-source fix | 684.0 | 681.1–686.8 | 2.906 |

Both candidate runs had zero request errors and matched the fixed-K greedy smoke on four prompts. The isolated FA3 graph reproducer in #62793 failed with mismatched padding and passed with aligned padding at split caps 1 and 32. These GPU results are from v0.31.0, **not this current-main checkout**. The instance was destroyed; current-main GPU validation, other backends and distributed configurations remain outstanding. The measured AV workload selected the full draft budget, so no trimming speedup is claimed.

## Details

At four requests and sixteen query tokens, the target AV graph pads to eight request slots while uniform draft prefill captures four slots. Draft prefill reuses the target attention metadata, including FA3 scheduler state whose layout depends on that padded batch size. Giving both paths the same varlen descriptor preserves the shared layout. The query-length bound allows bounded decode batches to select these graphs while keeping prefill-bearing batches on their fallback path. No GPU-to-CPU synchronization is added: the bound comes from the existing CPU scheduled-token array.

Duplicate-work checks found no open PR linked to #62793 or covering this shared target/draft-prefill padding fix. Nearby graph reachability and prefill-eligibility changes address different dispatch conditions. This PR does not change the general graph manager, metrics or the benchmark framework.

AI assistance was used for diagnosis, the candidate fix, tests and validation. The human submitter confirmed reviewing every changed line and personally running the focused CPU test command above before publication.

items.title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Cap varlen decode graph requests at the draft pass capacity
items.body:
## Overview

Fixes #62939. With DSpark adaptive verification, startup crashes when `max_num_seqs * num_query_per_req` exceeds `max_num_batched_tokens`. The issue's command (Qwen3-8B, `--max-num-batched-tokens 512`) on main:

```
Assertion `index out of bounds: 0 <= tl.broadcast_to(tmp29, [XBLOCK, R0_BLOCK]) < 40960` failed.
...
  File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py", line 1133, in capture_model
    self._dummy_run(**batch)
...
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered
```

`_dummy_run` caps requests at `max_num_batched_tokens // num_query_per_req` so the draft pass fits its buffers (#56448). But adaptive verification's startup profiling replays varlen decode graphs padded to `max_num_seqs` requests, and the drafter drafts for every padded slot: 256 * 7 query rows against 512-row buffers (#58984 clamps this only for DP > 1). This PR pads those graphs only up to the same cap, which the scheduler already enforces (#59468); configs where the cap does not bind are unchanged.

Not a duplicate: no open PR references #62939; #53970 takes a different route, growing the drafter buffers and the default budget.

## Validation

1x A100-80GB, base 6ee316eaea, Qwen3-8B + `dspark_qwen3_8b_block7`, `TRITON_ATTN`:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| the issue's `vllm serve` command | device-side assert at startup | starts, answers a chat request |
| 96 greedy chat requests at 512 | - | all complete, acceptance length 3.73 |
| `--max-num-batched-tokens 1792` (cap does not bind) | 51 varlen decode graphs | identical |

```
$ pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/dspark/test_dspark.py::test_dspark_adaptive_verification_with_small_token_budget
main:    1 failed (Engine core initialization failed, same assert)
```
