<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill.
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.
- [x] **Design Fit:** Keeps ordinary replay independent of Profile/Codec abstractions.
- [ ] **Testing and Validation:** Deferred by the user; no model/GPU validation yet.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Static checks pass; raw usage and limits documented.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Split boundary, dependency and validation gaps recorded.

</details>

items.title: [Feature][Spec Decode] Add Uno shared-model drafting with a draft-only LoRA adapter (Model Runner V2)
items.body:
**TL;DR.** Speculative decoding with no separate draft model: the target model drafts its own candidates through a small LoRA adapter, and vLLM's native rejection sampler verifies them. Measured against plain vLLM on the same card, same client and same serving shape: **2.1 to 2.4x single-stream on a GB10 and 1.7 to 1.9x on an RTX 3090** with this implementation, and **2.6x on an H100** with our earlier Model Runner V1 build of the same design, which this implementation beats in every cell measured side by side. It stays ahead under load (1.1 to 1.6x at four and sixteen streams on the GB10; 2.2x at eight streams and 1.7x at 32 on the H100). Output is lossless: greedy tokens match plain wherever plain reproduces itself, sampled-distribution tests pass, GSM8K is within one answer of plain. Uno stays out of vLLM's core files: outside its own modules the PR adds a two-line hook call in the V2 model runner, a five-line request check, and configuration. Tested on NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper (FlashAttention 2 and 3) and Blackwell, single GPU and tensor parallel, and on an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (ROCm, TRITON_ATTN). The reference SGLang implementation lands within 3% of the H100 build at every concurrency.

## Purpose

Adds native Uno self-drafting through `speculative_config.method="uno"` for Model Runner V2. One target model
produces `K` draft candidates per request from one base-weight seed row and `K-1` noise rows routed through the Uno
adapter; verification uses the native MRV2 rejection sampler. This follows the MRV2 direction agreed in
[RFC #55267](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55267). The earlier revision of this PR targeted Model Runner V1; this revision replaces it. Current head: reworked on 2026-10-11 so Uno stays out of vLLM's core files, on main at `ff440c7805`, then extended to AMD ROCm in Uno's own files; see the revision history below.

The change includes:

- A native MRV2 speculator that shares the target model, attention layers and KV cache with the drafter and applies the
  adapter only to noise rows, through the LoRA manager's public adapter-mapping call.
- Fused draft-input preparation in one kernel; the prompt length and the request count are runtime values, so it compiles once.
- Native request state, Gumbel sampling, verification, async scheduling and draft CUDA graphs; K lookahead KV slots
  with correct ownership at full acceptance, block boundaries, preemption and prefix-cache reuse. Near a request's length
  or context limit, the scheduler's existing per-request spec-token cap and lookahead cap apply; Uno adds no scheduler code.
- Startup and request validation (fail-closed for KV transfer, KV-sharing fast prefill, which would wrap the shared target and draft layers incorrectly and hand verification wrong prompt logits, pipeline/data/context parallelism, unsupported attention layouts, request-specific LoRA; tensor parallelism is supported and the draft uses the target's degree), a Qwen3-8B recipe ([the Uno docs page](https://github.com/brntech/vllm/blob/uno-core-upstream/docs/features/speculative_decoding/uno.md)), CPU regression tests and end-to-end model tests.

**Changes outside Uno's own files** (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/uno*.py`, its tests and docs):

| File | Lines | What |
|---|---:|---|
| `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py` | +2 | a generic `speculator.set_lora_manager(...)` call after the speculator loads |
| `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py` | +9 | that hook, a no-op on `BaseSpeculator` |
| `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/__init__.py` | +4 | the factory branch |
| `vllm/config/speculative.py` | +47 | the method, its fields and their validation |
| `vllm/config/vllm.py` | +10 / −2 | K lookahead slots, the async-scheduling allowlists, the V1 refusal |
| `vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py` | +5 | refuses a request-specific LoRA adapter with Uno |
| `.buildkite/test_areas/spec_decode.yaml` | +30 | the Uno jobs |
| `tests/v1/core/` | +269 | scheduler and prefix-caching cases for Uno's lookahead slots |

`scheduler.py`, `async_scheduler.py`, `sched/output.py` and `warmup.py` are unchanged. AMD support adds no line outside Uno's own files.

**Platforms.** Uno runs on NVIDIA GPUs with the `FLASH_ATTN` or `TRITON_ATTN` attention backend, and on AMD ROCm GPUs with `--attention-config '{"backend":"TRITON_ATTN"}'`. It restricts the attention backend, not the card: it admits exactly the backends its tests run, and any other attention backend (FlashInfer included), or on ROCm an unset backend, is refused when the config is validated, before weights load. A backend must also pass the capability checks Uno already had (native draft decode metadata updates; graph support for draft graphs), and `load_model` re-checks the backend each layer built. On ROCm, Uno has been tested on the Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201); `TRITON_ATTN` on NVIDIA on one RTX 3090 (sm_86).

Initial scope is NVIDIA GPUs (single GPU and tensor parallel) and AMD ROCm GPUs (tested single-GPU on the Radeon AI PRO R9700), text-only decoder models with one homogeneous full-attention KV group, the attention backends above, Model Runner V2 with async scheduling. A draft decode graph is captured only when some `cudagraph_capture_sizes` entry is at most `max_num_seqs * K`. The documented adapter is the original [`s-sahoo/uno-qwen3-8B`](https://huggingface.co/s-sahoo/uno-qwen3-8B) for `Qwen/Qwen3-8B`.

Uno is introduced in [Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04010); the method and adapter are credited to its authors. Development was assisted by AI tools, disclosed in the commit
trailers. A ready-to-run container of this revision is published at [github.com/brntech/vllm-uno](https://github.com/brntech/vllm-uno) (release v0.2.0, image `ghcr.io/brntech/vllm-uno:0.2.0`).

## Test Plan

Base: `ff440c7805` (main, 2026-10-10).

CPU (container, Python 3.12, no GPU):

```bash
pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_config.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_prepare_mrv2.py \
       tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_lora_mrv2.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_mrv2.py \
       tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_preemption.py -q
pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py \
       tests/v1/engine/test_preprocess_error_handling.py -k uno -q
pre-commit run --files $(git diff --name-only upstream/main HEAD)
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --all-files
```

GPU. Tested on NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell, single GPU and tensor parallel. The recorded Python-source overlay reproduces every GPU run on the base's per-commit CI image. Earlier revisions were run on a GB10 (Blackwell sm_121, ARM64), an H100 PCIe and an H100 NVL (FlashAttention 2 and 3), and at tensor-parallel 2 on two RTX 5090s (Blackwell sm_120); the current head was run on an RTX 3090 (Ampere sm_86) and an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, ROCm 7.2):

```bash
pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_prepare_mrv2.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_lora_mrv2.py -x -v
pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_gumbel_sample.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_rejection_sampler_utils.py \
  -k 'logits_cache or drafting_uses_a_separate_noise_stream or greedy_temperature_zero or gumbel_drafted_rejection_sample_is_unbiased or greedy_rejection_sample or chunked_requests_match_full_batch or placeholder_draft_token_rejected' \
  -v
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/test_uno.py -v -s
# The greedy matrix on TRITON_ATTN on NVIDIA:
VLLM_UNO_TEST_ATTENTION_BACKEND=TRITON_ATTN pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/test_uno.py::test_uno_greedy_matches_base_model -v -s
# On ROCm the e2e module runs on TRITON_ATTN by default:
pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_*.py tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/test_uno.py -v -s
```

## Test Result

### Throughput over plain vLLM

Every ratio is Uno divided by plain vLLM measured on the same card with the same client, model, precision and serving shape, in output tokens per second. GB10 and RTX 3090 figures are medians of three measured repeats after one warm-up; the H100 study reports mean per-prompt throughput at one stream and means of three warm batches at eight and 32 streams.

| Card | Workload | 1 stream | 4 / 8 streams | 16 / 32 streams |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| H100, earlier optimized MRV1 build (Qwen3-8B bf16, controlled, prefix caching off) | math | **2.58x** | 2.20x (8) | 1.74x (32) |
| GB10, this line at `49ffe316bb` (Qwen3-8B bf16, production shape) | short chat | **2.36x** | 1.31x (4) | 1.14x (16) |
| GB10 | long prompts | **2.21x** | 1.44x (4) | 1.15x (16) |
| GB10 | mixed | **2.06x** | 1.58x (4) | 1.12x (16) |
| RTX 3090, head `5da19391` (Qwen3-8B bf16, production shape) | short chat | **1.65x** | 1.18x (4) | 0.74x (16) |
| RTX 3090 | long prompts | **1.71x** | 1.13x (4) | 0.77x (16) |
| RTX 3090 | mixed | **1.85x** | 1.46x (4) | 0.72x (16) |

The H100 row is our earlier optimized Model Runner V1 implementation of the same design, measured in
[the study that IFM cites](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22652610) (single-prompt operating points on the same card: math 375 tokens/s, code 306, prose 212). The GB10 rows are this MRV2 line at `49ffe316bb` and the RTX 3090 rows head `5da19391`, both under one identical production shape (K=8, async scheduling, ctx 4096, `max_num_seqs` 16, 2048 batched tokens, 2 GiB KV, prefix caching, 128 output tokens). On the same GB10, with the optimized MRV1 release measured as a third arm, MRV2 exceeded it in all nine cells, by 1.03 to 1.31x. Uno is ahead wherever the card has compute headroom to verify drafts in: at four streams on every card, at sixteen on the GB10, at 32 on the H100. The reference SGLang implementation, measured on the same H100 against the same plain server, lands at 2.60x / 2.24x / 1.79x, within 3% of the H100 build at every concurrency.

### First-token latency

At head `5da19391`, same card, same client, median of three repeats: single-stream steady first token Uno 28.0 / 28.2 / 30.5 ms against plain 26.8 / 26.8 / 29.1 ms (short / mixed / long). The draft-input kernel takes the prompt length and the request count as runtime values, so it never recompiles for a new length or batch size. Since the rework there is no startup warmup of the draft sampler, so the first request compiles its sampler kernels.

### Lossless output

**Greedy exact-token matrix.** Seven K=1/K=8 cases (eager, CUDA graphs, prefix caching, dual-stream LoRA) compare Uno's greedy tokens with the plain engine's, each with a same-arm plain-vs-plain control. A first divergence is excused only where the plain engine's own top two raw logits are one bfloat16 step apart at that position, at most one prompt per batch, and every excused position is printed. Each case prints an instrument receipt (card, compute capability, graph mode, attention version, control coordinates, tie positions). At the current head the matrix also asserts that the attention implementation built is the requested backend's. RTX 3090, `TRITON_ATTN`: 7/7, every batch exact in tokens and text, no tie excused. RTX 3090, `FLASH_ATTN`: 7/7, exact except one excused tie in each of two cases (raw-logit gaps 0 and one bfloat16 step, at positions earlier rounds also met). R9700, `TRITON_ATTN`: 7/7, exact, no tie excused. Earlier heads: 7/7 on the GB10 and on the H100 under both FlashAttention 3 and 2.

**Context limit.** A nightly test serves four concurrent requests to `max_model_len` at K=8 and audits every draft KV slot against the limit and the request's block-table row; all four finish at exactly `max_model_len` with tokens and text equal to the plain engine's, and no draft row writes a slot at or past the limit.

**Sampled output.** Sampled-distribution permutation tests (256 samples for each of three prefixes, 16 tokens) pass for both Uno arms and for the independent plain-repeat control; raw greedy matches are 7/8 for both Uno arms against plain and 7/8 for plain against itself on a same-server repeat. GSM8K-128 (five-shot, temperature zero): plain 119/128, Uno MRV2 118/128, optimized MRV1 117/128.

### Request features under speculative decoding

Structured output (valid JSON from a `json_schema` request), logprobs, repetition and presence penalties and `ignore_eos` are all served with Uno drafting active. Min-p and logit bias are refused at admission by vLLM's general spec-decode guard, the same one EAGLE-3 hits. A request-specific LoRA adapter is refused before it is queued; a request can never select Uno's own adapter, including through a prebuilt `EngineCoreRequest` (a nightly test checks both, with exact outputs and the engine serving on).

### Continuous batching under KV pressure

The survivor test pins a 69-block KV pool, admits a seed request, two long peers and an abort peer, and asserts that a long peer is preempted while still generating and that its tokens after resumption equal its solo run. The pool is sized to force the crossing even when one long peer stalls at its admission footprint. It passed on the GB10, the H100 NVL (FlashAttention 3 and 2) and, at the current head, the RTX 3090 and the R9700. The test records the preemption at the scheduler's own event, resolves requests by the scheduler's internal ids, and writes its receipt to a file, so a non-firing run fails with a trace instead of skipping.

### Test counts

At the current head: CPU Uno modules 187 passed; pre-commit and mypy 3.12 clean (model runner V2 and factory 37, scheduler and prefix caching 391 at the previous head; this revision changes none of their files). The GPU rows below ran one local revision earlier; the only code change since removes an AMD chip check, so the unit suite now has one admission case fewer.

| Platform | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| RTX 3090 (sm_86), `FLASH_ATTN` | Uno unit tests | 202 passed |
| RTX 3090 (sm_86), `FLASH_ATTN` | nightly group: context limit + KV-slot audit, survivor, prebuilt LoRA | 3/3 |
| RTX 3090 (sm_86), `FLASH_ATTN` | 7-case greedy matrix | 7/7 (two excused bf16 ties) |
| RTX 3090 (sm_86), `TRITON_ATTN` | 7-case greedy matrix | 7/7, no excused ties |
| Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), `TRITON_ATTN` | Uno unit tests | 202 passed |
| Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), `TRITON_ATTN` | e2e module: matrix, context limit, survivor, prebuilt LoRA | 10/10, no excused ties |

No package dependencies are added. The Uno Buildkite job triggers on the spec-decode paths only and runs the greedy matrix; the context-limit, survivor and prebuilt-request tests run in a nightly job.

## Not in this patch

Three optimisations are left out to keep changes to vLLM's core files minimal. Each would first need a small generic hook, and can follow as a separate PR if wanted:

- **Early length-tail policy:** stop drafting on a step that may be a request's last, saving `K` lookahead KV rows near its length or context limit. Needs a per-request "next draft width" that a speculator can set.
- **Startup draft warmup:** compile the draft sampler's kernels at startup instead of on the first request. Needs a speculator warmup hook beside the existing dummy-propose warmup.
- **Cached LoRA metadata:** reuse precomputed adapter mappings for the draft rows instead of rebuilding them every step. Needs a public way to reuse a LoRA mapping.

Together they are worth about 2% at 16 concurrent requests on an RTX 3090 (Qwen3-8B, K=8, 16 greedy chats × 256 tokens, 3 repeats: 710.7 vs 726.2 tokens/s); single-stream is unchanged within noise (103.6 vs 104.4).

## Revision history

**2026-10-11, AMD ROCm.** Uno runs on AMD ROCm GPUs with `TRITON_ATTN` (tested on the Radeon AI PRO R9700, gfx1201), and on NVIDIA with `TRITON_ATTN` as well as `FLASH_ATTN`. It admits exactly the attention backends its tests run: any other backend, FlashInfer included, and an unset backend on ROCm, are refused when the config is validated, before weights load. Only Uno's own files change; the core footprint is unchanged. The greedy matrix asserts the attention implementation it built, and the survivor test no longer holds its in-process engine across the runner exit (only ROCm's teardown memory wait caught that reference).

**2026-10-11, rework.** Uno now stays out of vLLM's core files. `scheduler.py`, `async_scheduler.py`, `sched/output.py` and `warmup.py` are back to main; the V2 model runner change is a two-line call to a generic `set_lora_manager` speculator hook (a no-op on `BaseSpeculator`), and Uno's serving checks moved next to the method. Dropped: the early length-tail policy (the scheduler's existing per-request cap and lookahead cap keep the context limit correct, checked by a new nightly test that audits every draft KV slot), the startup draft warmup (the draft-input kernel takes the request count as a runtime value instead), and the cached LoRA-metadata restore (draft rows use the LoRA manager's public mapping call). A request-specific LoRA adapter is refused in the input processor, and no request can select Uno's own adapter. The greedy matrix counts ties in bfloat16 steps of the raw logits. The Uno CI job triggers on spec-decode paths only; the longer end-to-end tests run nightly.

**2026-10-10, merge of main `ff440c7805`.** Conflict resolved in the V2 model runner: #60754 moved the drafter hidden-state helper to `spec_decode.utils.get_drafter_hidden_states` and renamed `dp_sync` to `dp_sync_state`; Uno's proposal path and `propose()` follow both. API adaptations: #60736 (request-slot index mappings are int64; Uno's draft sample mapping follows, and the fused input preparation refuses a non-int64 one) and #57169 (packed KV layout: `BlockTables.kernel_block_sizes` is gone, so Uno's slot preparation reads `block_sizes`, without which the engine failed at warmup; the draft graph replay maps the kernel block table first). Method and scope are unchanged.

**2026-10-06, merge of main `385d86a6cf`.** Conflicts resolved in the V2 model runner (#40704) and in the imports of `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`. Method and scope are unchanged.

**2026-10-05, merge of main `74c5cbcd7b`.** Conflicts resolved in `vllm/config/vllm.py` (Uno's lookahead rule beside #59105's fill-in DSpark rule) and the V2 model runner (#57053, dynamic K: Uno requires a fixed `num_speculative_tokens` and `UnoSpeculator.propose` accepts the new argument). Method and scope are unchanged.

**2026-10-04, merge of main `84bcbc6264`.** Conflicts resolved in `spec_decode.yaml` (#57237's split), `tests/v1/core/utils.py`, `vllm/config/vllm.py` (`dflash` and `uno` on the async allowlists), the scheduler and the V2 model runner; adapted to #56497, #56807 and test-side changes from #55939, #58459, #58784 and #59359.

**2026-09-17, cleanup pass (on a fresh merge of main `91a4c40b45`).** The per-step timing tracer, the launch-key debug module and the JIT-monitor hooks were removed entirely, with their switches and scheduler-output fields.

**2026-09-16.** Merged with main at `af1c0149`; a pre-commit fix; DCO sign-off on the two commits.

**2026-09-14.** Model Runner V2 revision replaces the V1 revision; rebased onto main at `b87339888d`.

items.title: [MRV2][Spec Decode] Confidence stop for autoregressive drafting
items.body:
## Overview **+2.7% to +4.7% decode at c=1 on SPEED-Bench over the best fixed draft depth** (11 categories, four same-node runs, mean about +3.7%), within noise at c=4, GSM8K within run-to-run noise, on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 + MTP, one DGX Spark (SM121), with the NVFP4 draft head from #59973. Opt-in. While one request is decoding, `draft_confidence_threshold` turns `num_speculative_tokens` into a maximum depth: drafting stops once the drafter's top-1 probability falls below the threshold (the first draft is always kept), and only the drafted prefix is verified, using FULL CUDA graphs captured per verify length for a single request, as Dynamic SD (#32374) does per K. With more than one request the stop is off and the speculator drafts and verifies `draft_confidence_fallback_depth` tokens, with no readback. The stop reads only the drafter's distributions, never the drawn tokens, so rejection sampling stays exact. ```bash vllm serve --speculative-config '{"method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 6, "draft_confidence_threshold": 0.6, "draft_confidence_fallback_depth": 3}' ``` Model Runner V2, MTP/EAGLE/EAGLE3, SM121 only; any other configuration is rejected at startup. ## Results SPEED-Bench qualitative (32 prompts per category, greedy, 256 tokens), Flash-Next NVFP4, #59973 NVFP4 draft head, BF16 KV, both arms on one GB10 node (median SM clock 2522 MHz), one run per arm, measured on the final commit 7c4775ff31. Fixed 3 is the best fixed depth: in two other same-node sweeps fixed 4 was 0.1% and 0.6% slower, and on another node fixed 6 was 6.6% slower than fixed 3. | | fixed 3 drafts | confidence stop (max 6, fallback 3) | delta | |---|---:|---:|---:| | decode c=1, 11 categories | 49.1 tok/s (AL 2.80) | 50.5 tok/s (AL 3.07) | **+2.7%** | | decode c=4, 6 categories, per request | 33.0 tok/s | 32.6 tok/s | -1.2% | Per category at c=1: coding +16.7%, rag +9.0%, math +4.2%, multilingual +2.8%, writing +1.8%, roleplay +0.9%, qa +0.8%, reasoning +0.0%, stem -2.0%, humanities -2.1%, **summarization -7.7%**. Disclaimers: - Run to run spread is about 2%. Same-node c=1 runs of earlier commits with the same stop logic gave +4.4%, +2.9% and +4.7%; c=4 ranged from -1.2% to +1.0%. GSM8K (256) was 243 vs 246 and 244 vs 245 (fixed 3 first). - Before the fallback, the stop ran at every batch size and was 5.2% slower than fixed 3 at c=4; the fallback removes that. - Summarization regresses in every run (-3.7% to -9.0%). - The gain needs a cheap draft step: with the stock BF16 draft head the stop gains only +2.3% over 3 drafts.
Per category, c=1 (tok/s / AL) | category | Fixed 3 drafts | Confidence stop, max 6 | stop vs best fixed | |---|---:|---:|---:| | coding | 62.1 / 3.61 | 72.4 / 5.14 | +16.7% | | humanities | 42.9 / 2.50 | 42.0 / 2.40 | -2.1% | | math | 51.1 / 2.99 | 53.2 / 3.22 | +4.2% | | multilingual | 52.5 / 3.02 | 54.0 / 3.44 | +2.8% | | qa | 48.9 / 2.76 | 49.3 / 2.93 | +0.8% | | rag | 54.1 / 2.92 | 58.9 / 3.43 | +9.0% | | reasoning | 45.6 / 2.59 | 45.6 / 2.57 | +0.0% | | roleplay | 46.3 / 2.50 | 46.8 / 2.58 | +0.9% | | stem | 43.1 / 2.49 | 42.2 / 2.47 | -2.0% | | summarization | 49.4 / 2.88 | 45.6 / 3.01 | -7.7% | | writing | 44.7 / 2.50 | 45.5 / 2.57 | +1.8% | | average | 49.1 / 2.80 | 50.5 / 3.07 | +2.7% |
## Design questions raised on earlier attempts (#35301, #43522, #44885) - **Host sync.** The stop reads its chain flag after each draft step, but only when one request is decoding; with more requests there is no readback. On GB200 the readback made decode 24.7% slower (fixed 6: 378.4, stop: 284.8 tok/s), which is why it is SM121 only. A sync-free version is not cheap: about 65% of the gain is the shorter verify, so the host needs the drafted count, and reading it once per round was just as slow on GB200 (286.8). CUDA graph IF nodes can skip draft steps on the device (about 15 us each), but a device-side verify would need a switch over per-length verify graphs and device-side input preparation. - **Variable verify length.** Each verify length 1..K has its own FULL graph at batch size 1 (larger batches keep only the fallback and full lengths), so a shorter verify never replays a graph captured for another shape. Cost here: 13 FULL graphs instead of 5, 0.65 vs 0.45 GiB graph memory, capture time unchanged. Attention backends that only take an optimized path at a fixed spec-token count may run slower at the shorter lengths; this was measured with Qwen4Exp QSA/GDN only. - **Baselines and data.** Compared against the best fixed depth from a same-node sweep, on SPEED-Bench, not synthetic or ShareGPT prompts. - **Gains at higher batch.** The mean chain length flattens with batch size, so the stop only runs at one request. - **Hardware specific.** Yes: it helps where a draft step is long, which is why it is gated. SM120 (RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090) is untested. ## Not a duplicate - #35301 (same knob) and #28693 were closed as stale; #43522 and #44885 (confidence-based verify truncation for DFlash/PARD) were closed. - #52228 trims verify width from an online estimator and needs varlen attention backends, which Qwen4Exp QSA/GDN lack; it does not stop drafting. #52559 picks a per-step K for DFlash from past averages and reports no gain at c=1. - #32374 (Dynamic SD) picks K per batch-size range; at c=1 that is the fixed-depth baseline. Once its MTP drafter capture fix lands (#58821), a Dynamic SD schedule could drive the fallback depth instead of a separate key. ## Tests ```bash pytest -v tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_draft_confidence_stop.py \ tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dynamic_sd_cug.py \ tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_autoregressive_speculator.py pytest -v tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/mtp/qwen3_5/test_mtp.py -k confidence_stop ``` On GB10, at 7c4775ff31: 41 unit tests passed, and the e2e test passed (Qwen3.5-0.8B MTP, one request at a time, greedy outputs match fixed-depth MTP, AL at least 0.9x fixed 3). pre-commit and the mypy manual stage are clean. The serving numbers come from this branch applied with #59973 to a nightly 0cbac6cd1-based image. Size: about 220 source lines (84 in the new `confidence_stop.py`, 39 of config validation), 255 test lines, 7 doc lines. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the code, tests and benchmark harness; I reviewed every changed line and ran the measurements above. **Reproduction on upstream main (DGX Spark, GB10)** Upstream main 02b83919aa with the heads of #59958, #59973, #59740, #60068 and #54614 merged, no other runtime patches. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4, MTP 6 with confidence stop 0.6, sparse draft head via `draft_token_map` (32k ids, 16384 dynamic rows at rank 256, `draft_token_map_quantization: nvfp4`), FP8 KV, `host_file_gather` PLE tables. SPEED-Bench throughput 2K in / 1K out, fixed OSL, c=1, n=20: | Build | tok/s/user | AL | GSM8K-256 | |---|---|---|---| | upstream main + these PRs | 49.94 | 2.68 | 249/256 | | our internal stack, same node | 49.73 | 2.65 | 245/256 | The PR route reproduces the internal stack result within noise.

items.title: [Bugfix] Fix MiniMax M3 prompt reasoning initialization
items.body:
## Purpose

Fixes #46042.
Fixes #50549.

MiniMax-M3 adaptive reasoning can leak `<mm:think>` or `</mm:think>` into streaming `content` because parser initialization scans the entire rendered prompt. Instructional or example marker pairs can therefore make the parser conclude that reasoning already ended before generation starts.

This PR adds a prompt-boundary state hook and initializes MiniMax-M3 from `thinking_mode`: `enabled` starts in reasoning, `disabled` starts after reasoning, and `adaptive` lets generated output markers determine the state.

## Implementation summary

- preserves the existing reasoner behavior by default, with MiniMax-M3 overriding only prompt-boundary initialization
- carries the request-local reasoning state through Chat Completions, Responses, streaming parsing, structured output, offline chat, and batched serving
- keeps unresolved adaptive state deferred until generated tokens establish a boundary
- handles structured-output masks, alternative marker tokenizations, direct-content replay, continuation state, and parser reset after built-in tool turns

Although the visible symptom is parser-level, the state has to cross each place that creates or reuses a reasoning parser. Otherwise one serving path can fall back to the old full-prompt scan or leak continuation state between requests.

<details>
<summary>Detailed implementation scope</summary>

- uses `is_reasoning_end_from_prompt()` in online, offline, Responses, streaming, and structured-output initialization
- scopes deferred adaptive marker checks to generated tokens so prompt examples cannot activate the grammar
- allows grammar-valid tokens plus every decoded reasoning-marker tokenization while adaptive state is unresolved
- replays direct adaptive content through the grammar, including ambiguous prefixes and speculative draft state
- derives continuation state from the final assistant message only and preserves open or closed `thinking` content parts
- propagates incomplete Responses reasoning items to frontend and engine parsers
- clears continuation-only state and refreshes the frontend parser after Responses built-in tool turns rerender the prompt
- keeps batch parsers request-local and initializes each engine-side structured-output parser from its prompt once

</details>

## Review focus

1. Default compatibility of `is_reasoning_end_from_prompt()` and the MiniMax-M3 `thinking_mode` override
2. Deferred adaptive transitions in structured output, including generated-token-only checks and marker tokenization boundaries
3. Request isolation and continuation reset across Responses, batch, offline chat, and built-in tool turns

## Validation

Local focused validation:

- MiniMax-M3 reasoning parser: 44 passed
- reasoning-aware structured output: 21 passed
- offline chat prompt-state forwarding: 1 passed
- batch prompt-state forwarding: 3 passed
- Responses serving: 23 passed, 1 expected xfail
- `ruff check`, `ruff format`, Python `compileall`, and `git diff --check` passed

The 92 focused tests ran in a CPU-only temporary environment with `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=empty`.

External MiniMax-M3 validation:

- [Parser validation on aarch64](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50594#issuecomment-5281778580): 44/44 parser tests passed and the deployed prompt-state failure was reproduced and confirmed
- [Production end-to-end validation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50594#issuecomment-5290659689): the streaming marker leak was fixed on both OpenAI and Anthropic-compatible APIs, Anthropic streaming `thinking` blocks were restored, and tool calls remained working

The production deployment backported the parser, chat utility, and serving call-site changes rather than running the complete 17-file branch. The remaining Responses, batch, offline, and structured-output paths are covered by the focused CPU tests above and still need repository CI.

## Current CI status

The current `pre-run-check` is stopped by the first-contributor authorization gate, and the pre-commit job was skipped. CI requires a `verified`, `ready`, or `ready-run-all-tests` label, or a trusted reviewer action such as `/ci run`. Repository-wide GPU CI has not run yet.

## Related work

- #45718 fixed split-token MiniMax-M3 marker parsing, but not prompt-boundary state initialization.
- #50152 identified the same full-prompt scan failure and demonstrated the production symptom, but closed without merging.
- #48550 also addresses prompt-mode initialization while adding broader speculative-decoding and tool-parser changes.
- This PR is limited to prompt-boundary reasoning initialization and the state propagation needed to preserve it across supported serving paths.

<details>
<summary>Focused test commands</summary>

```bash
uv run pytest -q tests/reasoning/test_minimax_m3_reasoning_parser.py tests/v1/structured_output/test_reasoning_structured_output.py
uv run pytest -q tests/entrypoints/llm/test_offline_reasoning_state.py
uv run pytest -q tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_batched_chat_completions.py -k batch_forwards_prompt_reasoning_state
uv run pytest -q tests/entrypoints/openai/responses/test_serving_responses.py
```

</details>

## AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation and regression-test drafting. The commits include `Assisted-by` trailers. The submitter requested the changes after reviewing the proposed scope.

items.title: [Feature]: Add DFly speculative decoding and D-Cut support（Related to issue 50245）
items.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Motivation

We would like to propose adding DFly speculative decoding support to vLLM, together with D-Cut, a dynamic draft pruning method for speculative decoding.

DFly is the main speculative decoding method in this proposal. Existing DFlash/DSpark-style paths are treated as baselines or compatibility foundations. The primary goal is to make DFly usable in vLLM's standard serving stack and improve its runtime efficiency with D-Cut.

## Feature overview

This proposal focuses on two main features:

### 1. DFly speculative decoding

DFly is a speculative decoding method that uses a draft model to generate candidate tokens for the target model to verify.

The proposed integration adds support for running DFly-style draft models inside vLLM, including:

- recognizing DFly draft model architectures
- registering the DFly draft model implementation
- routing DFly through the speculative decoding runtime
- supporting the required draft-token transport and verification flow
- keeping compatibility with existing speculative decoding infrastructure

The expected result is that users can serve target models with a DFly draft model through normal vLLM APIs, without relying on an external or out-of-tree runtime.

### 2. D-Cut dynamic draft pruning

D-Cut is a dynamic pruning strategy for speculative decoding.

Instead of always verifying a fixed number of draft tokens, D-Cut chooses how many draft tokens to keep for each request based on draft confidence and runtime cost. This helps avoid wasting verification compute on low-confidence draft tokens.

At a high level, D-Cut provides:

- per-request dynamic keep-length selection
- confidence-based draft pruning
- scheduler-side truncation of draft tokens
- keep-ratio metrics
- optional cost-aware automatic mode
- integration with the DFly speculative decoding path

D-Cut is intended to improve the efficiency of DFly by adapting the verification width to each request.

## Why this is useful

Speculative decoding performance depends heavily on both draft quality and verification cost. A fixed draft length can be suboptimal:

- if the draft model is confident, verifying more tokens may be beneficial
- if the draft model is uncertain, verifying too many draft tokens wastes target-model compute
- different requests in the same batch may need different draft lengths

DFly provides the draft generation path, while D-Cut makes the verification process adaptive.

Together, they aim to improve serving efficiency while keeping the integration inside vLLM's existing speculative decoding framework.

## Expected behavior

After this feature lands, users should be able to:

1. Configure a DFly draft model for speculative decoding in vLLM.
2. Run DFly through the standard vLLM serving/runtime path.
3. Enable D-Cut to dynamically prune draft tokens.
4. Observe D-Cut keep-ratio metrics.
5. Compare DFly + D-Cut against baseline speculative decoding methods.

## Suggested upstreaming plan

To make review easier, this could be split into several PRs:

1. Add DFly model registration and config handling.
2. Add the DFly speculative decoding runtime path.
3. Add D-Cut dynamic pruning logic.
4. Add D-Cut metrics and cost-aware mode.
5. Add minimal tests and benchmark examples for DFly + D-Cut.

We would like feedback from maintainers on whether DFly and D-Cut fit vLLM's speculative decoding roadmap, and how the implementation should be split for upstream review.


### Alternatives

1. Add DFly first and upstream D-Cut later, although D-Cut is an important part of making DFly efficient.

2. Use a fixed draft length instead of D-Cut, but fixed-length verification is less adaptive to per-request draft confidence and runtime cost.

### Additional context

Other speculative decoding methods in the branch are mainly used as baselines or compatibility foundations. The two main features proposed in this issue are:

- DFly speculative decoding
- D-Cut dynamic draft pruning

The implementation can be cleaned up and split into smaller PRs based on maintainer feedback.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

Related to #50245

items.title: [Core][CUDA Graph] Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes
items.body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

**Problem.** A CUDA graph replays a recorded step so the CPU does not launch each kernel. A batch with no graph of its size runs eagerly, and at serving batch sizes the CPU launching kernels, not the GPU, sets its speed. In model runner V2, one token list decides which batch sizes get graphs, for both prefill and decode. With speculative decoding each decode request carries 1 + K tokens, so a 1024-token list covers only 1024/(1+K) decode requests: 128 at K=7, while servers run up to 1024. On GB200, the models we validated spend 22–73% of engine time in such eager steps.

**Change.** Separate settings for prefill graphs, in tokens, and for decode graphs, in requests, each with its own cap. The old fields keep working, deprecated.
- Off SM100 the split keeps main's behavior, apart from the differences listed below.
- On SM100 (GB200/B200) each kind is sized on its own: decode graphs cover every batch size the scheduler can form, and prefill graphs reach 8192 tokens. That is where the speedup comes from.

This is the "separate prefill/decode graph sizes" item of the Q4 roadmap (#61024).

## Claims

On 4× GB200 with 256 concurrent requests:
- Throughput is ×1.3–3.2 of main on six MoE configurations and ×0.98–0.99 on a dense model.
- GSM8K answers match main within noise.
- KV cache is 0.63–0.98 of main. On DeepSeek most of the gap is today's memory estimate over-reserving; the rest is the sparse indexer's decode logits in the widest decode graph. See "KV cache on DeepSeek" under Differences from main; the fixes are listed in Follow-ups (memory estimate, a fair KV comparison, and the indexer logits).

## Configuration

### The four fields

They live on `CompilationConfig` (`--compilation-config '{...}'`) and come in two independent pairs.

| field | unit | what it controls | default on SM100 | default on other GPUs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens` | tokens | Cap: the largest prefill, chunked-prefill or mixed batch that runs as a CUDA graph (PIECEWISE). | `min(8192, max_num_batched_tokens)` | 512, as on main |
| `prefill_cudagraph_capture_token_sizes` | tokens | The exact token counts that get a prefill graph. Overrides the default grid. | 103 sizes up to 8192: main's grid up to 1024, then every 256 tokens up to 4096 and every 512 up to 8192 | main's list |
| `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests` | requests | Cap: the largest uniform decode batch, in requests, that runs as a FULL graph. | `max_num_seqs` (1024 with `vllm serve` on GB200) | main's request counts, 512 / (1 + K) |
| `decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes` | requests | The exact request counts that get a decode graph. Overrides the default grid. | every count up to 32, then 16 sizes per doubling (every 2 up to 64, every 4 up to 128, …): 112 sizes at 1024 | main's request counts |

**Graphs captured with the defaults.** GB200 `vllm serve`: `max_num_seqs` 1024, `max_num_batched_tokens` 16384, `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`. Each cell is the number of graphs, with the widest in parentheses.

| graphs | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| prefill, PIECEWISE | 83 (1024 tokens) | 103 (8192 tokens) |
| decode, FULL, no speculative decoding | 83 (1024 requests) | 112 (1024 requests) |
| EAGLE3 K=7: target decode, FULL | 80 (128 requests) | 112 (1024 requests) |
| EAGLE3 K=7: draft prefill, PIECEWISE / FULL | 83 / 80 | 103 / 112 |
| EAGLE3 K=7: one-token draft decode, FULL | 83 (1024 requests) | 112 (1024 requests) |
| DSpark K=7: target decode / DSpark, FULL | 80 (128) / 80 (144 requests) | 112 (1024) / 112 (1024 requests) |

**Memory per kind.** Each kind of graph costs memory in two places:
- **Graph objects:** the driver's memory for each instantiated graph (`cudaGraphExec`), outside the torch allocator. There is one per graph, so it grows with the count: 15–18 MiB per PIECEWISE size, 10–18 MiB per target FULL graph, 0.4–1.2 MiB per drafter graph. Capture takes 1–1.5 s per PIECEWISE size (two passes), 0.5 s per target FULL graph and 10–50 ms per drafter graph.
- **Its widest graph's tensors, in the graph pool.** All graphs share one private pool of the torch allocator, which holds the tensors their kernels pass to each other. Graphs are captured widest first and the narrower ones reuse the freed blocks. So a kind needs the pool only as large as its widest graph, and the pool is the largest of these needs, not their sum.

Measured per GPU on rank 0 (rank 3 agrees within 2 MiB), main and this PR on one node, the 60a7d568f4 wheel, the PR validation's serve commands. DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DSpark K=7, TP4+EP, is the largest case:

| GiB | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| **target prefill, PIECEWISE** | 83 graphs, up to 1024 tokens | 103 graphs, up to 8192 tokens |
| ↳ graph objects | 1.60 | 2.01 |
| ↳ widest graph's tensors | 0.19 | 1.55 |
| **target decode, FULL** | 80 graphs, up to 128 requests × 8 tokens | 112 graphs, up to 1024 requests × 8 tokens |
| ↳ graph objects | 1.33 | 1.79 |
| ↳ widest graph's tensors | 1.70 | 13.58 |
| ↳ of which the sparse indexer's decode logits | 1.50 | 12.02 |
| **DSpark draft decode, FULL** | 80 graphs, up to 144 requests | 112 graphs, up to 1024 requests |
| ↳ graph objects | 0.06 | 0.10 |
| ↳ widest graph's tensors | 0.57 | 4.05 |
| **graph pool, all streams** | 4.33 | 22.11 |
| ↳ of which aux hidden states kept by every PIECEWISE size (below) | 0.82 | 2.74 |
| ↳ of which DSpark's own capture stream (below) | 0.74 | 5.23 |
| default pool and other memory added by capture | 0.29 | 1.18 |
| **the real capture** (the log's `actual`) | **5.81** | **24.79** |
| **all graph memory at rest**, with the PIECEWISE objects | **8.0** | **27.4** |

- The parts overlap inside the pool (a graph reuses blocks freed by wider ones), so they do not add up to the totals; each total is measured.
- The PIECEWISE objects are allocated in the profiling pass and kept for the process lifetime, so the log's `actual` leaves them out.
- A pool can reserve more than its widest graph needs: main's widest decode graph needs 1.70 GiB but reserves 2.67, because its FP32 indexer logits took a second segment through fragmentation.
- This PR's "default pool and other" is mostly persistent output buffers sized for 8192 tokens (0.25 against 0.03 GiB) and free space pinned in their segments.
- **The decode width is the one large cost, and only DeepSeek pays it:** its widest decode graph holds the sparse indexer's decode logits, `max_model_len` / 4 × 6 B per token. To give memory back, lower `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests` (see "How to use them"). Sharing one logits buffer between graphs and eager steps is listed under Follow-ups.
- **With both changes below,** this PR's pool measures 14.1 GiB: the PIECEWISE graphs and DSpark's fit inside the widest decode graph. A prefill-only instance's pool measures 2.1 GiB.
- **MiniMax-M3, EAGLE3 K=3, TP4** (main → this PR, GiB): PIECEWISE objects 1.38 → 1.93; target and EAGLE3 FULL objects 0.91 → 1.31; graph pool 1.80 → 5.84, of which aux hidden states 1.22 → 4.09 and EAGLE3's own capture streams 0.30 → 0.85; the real capture 3.15 → 8.13; all graph memory at rest 4.6 → 10.2. With both changes, this PR's whole pool is its widest PIECEWISE graph, 1.9 GiB.
- **Off SM100** (H100/H200 defaults), prefill and target decode keep main's 51 / 51 graphs. Only the one-token draft decodes grow, from 51 to 112.

With an EAGLE3, DSpark or DFlash drafter, two more behaviors add memory. Both exist on main too. The first grows with the captured PIECEWISE tokens and the second with the drafter's widest graph, so both cost more on this PR:
- **Every PIECEWISE size keeps its own aux hidden states.**
  - These drafters read three of the target's intermediate hidden states. The target's PIECEWISE graph returns them as `(hidden_states, [aux, ...])`.
  - After each capture, the graph wrapper turns its output into weak references, so that the next size can reuse the output's memory in the pool. `weak_ref_tensors` converts only the outer tuple, so the inner list stays a strong reference.
  - Each captured size then holds 3 × tokens × hidden × 2 B for the life of the engine: 192 MiB at 8192 tokens on DeepSeek-V4. The total grows with the sum of all captured PIECEWISE tokens, not with the widest.
  - Keeping a copy per size does not look necessary. The drafter copies the aux states right after the target's replay, before any other graph replays, and the `hidden_states` output, already weak, relies on the same order. Letting `weak_ref_tensors` recurse frees them (https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb), with the same GSM8K answers and acceptance on DeepSeek-V4 and M3.
- **Drafter graphs cannot reuse the target's free memory in the pool.**
  - The target and each drafter capture through their own `CudaGraphManager.capture()`, and each call opens a new CUDA stream (`graph_capture()`). They all capture into the same pool.
  - The caching allocator hands a free block only to requests on the stream that allocated it. So the drafter's widest graph reserves new memory for its whole peak, even when the pool has enough free, and its narrower graphs reuse that. In effect the drafter gets its own share of the pool.
  - On DeepSeek-V4 DSpark K=7, DSpark's widest graph reserved 5.35 GiB while the pool held 14.2 GiB free. On M3, EAGLE3's graphs add 0.84 GiB.
  - #59537 (open) captures with one stream per device; then DSpark's graphs fit inside the target's pool. It should land with the aux-state change: without that change and without NUMA binding, it slowed breakable PIECEWISE steps 1.2–1.6× in 4 of 4 launches, cause open.

**Rules.**
- A cap alone captures the default grid up to the cap. A list alone captures exactly those sizes; sizes above `max_num_batched_tokens` (prefill) or `max_num_seqs` (decode) are dropped with a warning.
- With both a list and its cap, the list's max must not exceed the cap. A follow-up will require them to match, as main does for the old pair.
- `[]` captures none of that kind. Both `[]` turns CUDA graphs off.
- The pairs are independent: setting one never changes the other's graphs.
- Under `cudagraph_mode` FULL or PIECEWISE, which do not separate decode batches, every batch uses the prefill sizes.

### How to use them

The defaults suit most deployments. Change a cap when one of these applies:

```bash
# KV cache is short, e.g. DeepSeek-V4 at long context: decode graphs up to 512 requests.
# Prefill graphs are unchanged. Measured: about 6 GiB back, 5-11% slower at 1024 concurrent requests.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests": 512}'

# MoE model at DP = 1 with 8K+ prompts: prefill graphs up to 16K tokens (needs max_num_batched_tokens >= 16384).
# Measured: up to 25% less engine time. With EAGLE3 or DSpark drafters it costs 2-8 GiB more while every PIECEWISE size keeps its own aux hidden states.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 16384}'

# Dense model at small TP: graphs above about 1.5K tokens neither help nor hurt there; this saves startup time.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 2048}'

# Prefill instance in a prefill/decode disaggregated deployment: it runs no decode batches.
vllm serve <model> --compilation-config '{"decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes": []}'
```

The default grids are tuned: the decode grid pads by at most 0.6% of target time, and the prefill grid by about 1%. An exact list replaces them, so set one only for batch sizes you know the deployment runs. A sparse list pads: a power-of-two decode list loses 3–4.5% of engine time against the default grid.

### With speculative decoding

A decode size is a request count. Each runner turns it into tokens with its own query length `q`:

| runner | `q` | graph for `decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes=[64]` at K = 7 |
|---|---|---|
| target | 1 + K | 512 tokens |
| EAGLE / EAGLE3 / MTP draft steps after the first | 1 | 64 tokens |
| DSpark | K | 448 tokens |
| DFlash, multi-module MTP | K + 1 | 512 tokens |

- **Decode coverage no longer shrinks as K grows.** The graph's width does grow: 1024 requests at K = 7 is an 8192-token graph.
- **One-token draft steps always cover `max_num_seqs`**, even when the target's decode cap is lower; only `[]` turns them off. Each of their K − 1 eager steps would otherwise pay its host launches.
- **Multi-token drafters (DSpark, DFlash, multi-module MTP) follow the target's decode sizes.** Extending them waits for #59537, which lets their graphs share the target's memory pool.
- **Dynamic speculative decoding** (`num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size`): each tier gets the request counts its schedule reaches, at its own `q`.

### With adaptive verification

Adaptive-verification decode batches mix query lengths, so they take token-keyed FULL graphs on the prefill grid. These go up to `min(max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests × (1 + K), max_num_batched_tokens)` tokens: lowering the decode cap also narrows them. On DeepSeek-V4.1 (K = 5, 1024 requests) the widest is 6144 tokens.

### Migrating from the old fields

**Nothing breaks.** `cudagraph_capture_sizes` and `max_cudagraph_capture_size` still work on model runner V2 and capture what they captured on main, with a deprecation warning. Only mixing old and new fields in one config is an error. Model runner V1 is unchanged.

**To switch,** delete the old field and the defaults above apply. To set the caps yourself, give each kind its own value: prefill in tokens, decode in requests.

```bash
# Before: one cap for both kinds, in tokens.
--compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size": 1024}'

# After: prefill graphs up to 1024 tokens, and a decode graph for every batch up to max_num_seqs (here 1024).
--compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 1024, "max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests": 1024}'
```

## Why this design

**Why not just raise the cap on main.** One list serves both kinds, so covering decode drags prefill along at main's fine spacing.
- At K=7, `max_cudagraph_capture_size=8192` makes main capture 531 PIECEWISE sizes (one every 16 tokens above 256) and 528 FULL decode graphs for 1024 sequences.
- At the per-graph costs measured here, that is about 16–18 GiB of graph-exec memory and 12–18 minutes of capture (estimated, not run).
- The right cap also moves with K: 8192 tokens is 1024 requests at K=7 but 512 at K=15.

This PR covers the same range with 103 PIECEWISE and 112 FULL decode graphs.

**Prefill cap: 8192.** Measured on the MoE models this PR targets. Engine time is for 8K-token prompts with 1K output tokens at 16 concurrent requests, with the 16K cap = 1.00 (lower is faster). PIECEWISE graph memory is per GPU, as of today.

| model, parallelism | prefill graphs pay off up to | engine time at cap 8K / 12K / 16K | PIECEWISE graph memory at 8K / 12K / 16K |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4+EP | 15–16K tokens | 1.33 / 1.00 / 1.00 | 3.0 / 5.0 / 7.7 GiB |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, TP4+EP | ~16.5K | 1.13 / 1.02 / 1.00 | 3.2 / 5.8 / 6.4 GiB |
| MiniMax-M3, TP4 | 12.5–13.8K | 1.20 / 0.99 / 1.00 | 4.8 / 8.0 / 12.4 GiB |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DP4+EP | ~9K | 1.14 / 1.02 / 1.00 | 3.6 / 6.5 / 9.4 GiB |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DP4+EP | – | **0.86** / 1.00 / 1.00 | 8.4 / 12.3 / 16.2 GiB |

Why 8192:
- **Every MoE model keeps gaining from prefill graphs well past main's 1024-token cap** (9–16.5K tokens), so the cap must go up.
- **8192 is the largest cap that gains on every config measured and regresses none.** Two problems make 12K and 16K a trade today:
  - PIECEWISE graph memory grows with the cap: 8K → 16K adds 4.7 GiB on DeepSeek-V4 TP4+EP and 7.6 GiB on M3, because every PIECEWISE size keeps its own aux hidden states (see "Where the memory goes"; main does the same).
    - Freeing them (https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb) brings the increase down to +2.0 and +1.3 GiB.
  - With DP > 1 and a gather-based MoE path (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next DP4+EP), any cap above 8K is 14–20% slower, because each rank computes the other ranks' padded rows. That needs the gather-based MoE to skip padded rows, which no open PR does.
- **Next step:** once the aux-state change lands, raise the default to 16K at DP = 1, for up to 25% less engine time on long prompts. Keep 8192 at DP > 1 until the gather-based MoE skips padded rows.
- A dense model is not the target. A dense 27B at TP1 stops gaining at about 1.5K, and larger graphs neither help nor hurt it, so the default is harmless there.

**Decode cap: `max_num_seqs`.** Main divides its 1024-token list by 1 + K, so the share of decode batch sizes that get a graph falls as K grows. This PR covers every batch size the scheduler can form, at any K.

![Decode FULL graph hit rate: this PR hits a graph at every batch size up to max_num_seqs at any K; main stops at 1024 / (1 + K) requests](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pb314314/vllm/cg-pr-assets/decode_full_graph_hit_rate.png)

| K | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main: largest decode batch with a graph | 512 | 341 | 256 | 170 | 128 |
| this PR | 1024 | 1024 | 1024 | 1024 | 1024 |

Decode steps are launch-bound at every batch size, so every batch should get a graph. The cost is the widest graph's memory; see "How to use them".

The table of all defaults and the measurements behind them, including the choice of decode grid, are under Details.

**Commits.**
1. Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes.
2. Default to wider CUDA graphs on SM100.
3. One-token draft decode graphs cover `max_num_seqs`.
4. Disable CUDA graphs when no capture size is left.
5. Bound decode graphs by the recorded max capture size.
6. Keep GPT-OSS's decode coverage under dynamic speculative decoding.
7. Bound KDA recoverSSM mixed graphs by 1 + K tokens per request.

## Differences from main

**Gains**
- **SM100 defaults.**
  - Prefill graphs go to `min(8192, max_num_batched_tokens)` tokens (main: 1024).
  - Decode graphs go to `max_num_seqs` requests at any K (main: 1024/(1+K)).
  - Adaptive verification's cap grows with them (K = 5, 512 sequences: 1024 → 3072 tokens).
- **One-token draft decodes reach `max_num_seqs` on every GPU** (main: the token cap, 512 off SM100). Off SM100 the recorded `max_cudagraph_capture_size` rises with them, from 512 to `max_num_seqs`. Backends that size graph buffers by it take about 2 MiB more.
- **Dynamic speculative decoding.** Each tier gets its own graphs, graphs a tier can never reach are dropped, and no tier loses coverage.
- **Explicit deprecated lists.** Decode graphs gain coverage.

**Losses and costs**
- **KV cache on DeepSeek: 0.65 (V4) and 0.63 (V4.1) of main. Most of the gap is the memory estimate, not graph memory.** Per GPU:

  | config | graph memory, actual: main → PR | reserved by the estimate: main → PR | KV PR / main |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DSpark K=7 | 5.81 → 24.79 GiB | 8.56 → 46.46 GiB | 0.65 |
  | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, DSpark K=5 + adaptive verification, 256K | 33.38 → 31.43 GiB | 25.36 → 47.38 GiB | 0.63 |

  - **DeepSeek-V4.1:** the PR's graphs use 2 GiB less than main's. The whole gap is the estimate.
    - On the PR it over-reserves by 16 GiB, which #59368 fixes.
    - On main it under-reserves by 8 GiB, because adaptive verification's profiling cache is not counted (#61509). Main's KV there is not safe.
  - **DeepSeek-V4:** the PR reserves 37.9 GiB more than main.
    - About 19 GiB of that is the estimate over-reserving: 21.7 GiB on the PR, against 2.75 on main.
    - The other 19 GiB is real. These parts are derived from per-kind measurements:
      - About 10.5 GiB is the sparse indexer's decode logits in the widest decode graph: 1024 × 8 rows × 262,144 × 6 B at 1M context. Main's eager path needs the same buffer at high concurrency but does not budget it, so main OOM-crashes at 1024 concurrent requests (#62860).
      - About 4.6 GiB is the DSpark drafter's widest graph, which cannot reuse the target's free pool memory until #59537.
      - About 1.9 GiB is the aux hidden states every PIECEWISE size keeps (https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb).
      - About 1 GiB is the graph-exec memory of the extra graphs.
  - **Workaround today:** `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests=512` gives back about 6 GiB, for 5–11% at 1024 concurrent requests.
- **The widest one-token draft graph holds the drafter's logits.** That is +0.25–0.37 GiB for EAGLE3 and MTP drafters, and +1.02 GiB for Gemma 4 E2B's 262k vocabulary. No cap limits only the drafter; adding one is a follow-up.
- **DSpark off SM100.** Its graphs (`q = K`) follow the target's request cap (`q = K + 1`), so they cover about K/(K+1) of main's requests. Max draft requests, main → this PR:

  | K | 7 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 1 |

### Motivation: what a CUDA graph buys, what it costs

**What it buys: host launch time.** An eager step costs roughly max(host launch time, GPU time). A graph replay removes almost all of the host part.
- **Decode steps** are launch-bound at serving batch sizes, so a FULL decode graph always pays off. On Qwen3-8B EAGLE3 K=7, the six draft steps of one decode step take 6.2–7.0 ms of host time eagerly, against 0.17 ms for one replay (measured on builds with per-step tracing).
- **Prefill and mixed steps** are launch-bound only up to a crossover size, s* ≈ T_launch / g, where g is the GPU time per token per rank. Past s* the GPU work hides the launches, and a PIECEWISE graph gains nothing.
  - Measured on GB200: about 15–16K tokens on DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP4+EP, about 16.5K on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next TP4+EP, 12.5–13.8K on MiniMax-M3 TP4, and about 1.5K on a dense 27B model at TP1.
  - So the useful prefill cap depends on the model, the hardware and the parallelism, not on the decode width.

**What it costs**, per graph kind:
- **Graph-pool memory comes from the widest graph, not the number of graphs.** Every graph of a process is captured into one shared pool, and later graphs reuse the blocks earlier graphs freed.
- **The number of graphs costs graph-exec memory and startup time:**
  - each PIECEWISE size: 15–18 MiB, and 0.45–0.74 s in each of the two capture passes;
  - each target FULL graph: about 16 MiB and 0.5 s;
  - each drafter graph: 0.5–1.2 MiB and 10–50 ms.

So graph count is cheap, and graph width is what has to be weighed.

**Why one list does not work.** The token list mixes two different quantities:
- **It sizes prefill graphs in tokens**, which is the right unit for them.
- **It caps decode graphs at `T / (1 + K)` requests**, where K is the number of speculative tokens. The decode coverage therefore shrinks as K grows. Each runner also rounds the list to its own query length.
- **Raising one kind's coverage raises the other's.** Getting decode graphs to 1024 requests at K=7 needs an 8192-token cap. On main that cap also means 531 PIECEWISE sizes at its fine spacing (see Overview).
- **On GB200 with main, the models we validated spend 22–73% of engine time in eager steps.** Those steps are mixed steps above the 1024-token cap and decode batches above 1024/(1+K) requests.

### Prefill graphs (tokens)

- **What is captured.** Token-keyed graphs, PIECEWISE under `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`.
- **Default on SM100 (commit 2).** Up to `min(8192, max_num_batched_tokens)` tokens.
  - The grid is main's up to 1024 tokens (1, 2, 4, then steps of 8 up to 256 and steps of 16), then steps of 256 up to 4096, then steps of 512.

- **Default on other GPUs, and with the deprecated fields.** Main's list, 51 graphs up to 512 tokens.
- **Why 8192.** It is below every measured s* except the dense TP1 model's. On that model, prefill graphs above s* neither help nor hurt (engine time 0.996–0.998 of the 16K cap).
  - 16K would be better for single-DP MoE models on 8K-prompt workloads, by 13–33%. An 8K chunk plus the decodes that ride along lands just above 8192, so at 8192 it runs eagerly. A replicate with two server instances per cap on DeepSeek-V4-Flash TEP, 8K/1K at concurrency 16, gives 8192 / 16384 engine time 1.357 (sd 0.032, n = 12).

- **Why this grid.** Steps of 256 and 512 above 1024 keep padding near 1% on the TP4 MoE models. Halving the steps gains 0.3–0.4% and costs 28 more graphs.
- **Cost.**
  - The 20 extra graphs add about 20–30 s of startup and 0.3–0.4 GiB of graph-exec memory.

### Decode graphs (requests)

- **What is captured.** FULL graphs for uniform decode batches, keyed by request count. Each runner uses its own query length:
  - the target: `q = 1 + K`;
  - one-token draft decodes: `q = 1`;
  - DSpark: `q = K`;
  - DFlash and multi-module MTP: `q = K + 1`.
- **Default on SM100 (commit 2).** Up to `max_num_seqs` requests at any K. The grid has every count up to 32, then 16 sizes per doubling (every 2 up to 64, every 4 up to 128, …). That is 112 graphs at `max_num_seqs` 1024.
  - Main covers 1024/(1+K) requests: 128 at K=7, 256 at K=3.
- **Default on other GPUs, and with the deprecated fields.** Main's request counts: what main's token list holds at the target's `q`. At K=7 that is 48 graphs up to 64 requests.
- **Why up to `max_num_seqs`.** Then every decode batch the scheduler can form has a FULL graph.
  - The cost is width. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DSpark K=7, 1K/1K, concurrency 1024, equal KV, three launches per arm), capping at 512 instead of 1024 requests saves 6.0 GiB per GPU and costs about 5% throughput (11% counting a third launch that ran slow throughout, cause open). All of that is the DSpark drafter's eager fallback: with the target at 512 and DSpark at 1024, throughput equals 1024 / 1024 (0.999).
  - Decode-only steps above the cap run PIECEWISE, about 7% slower each. On a decode-heavy 1K/4K concurrency 1024 the cap at 512 costs nothing measurable (0.986, two launches per arm). The 1K/1K cost comes from host-bound mixed steps.
  - Users who need the KV can lower `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests`.
- **Why this grid.** Padded rows are not free.
  - A padded row costs 0.56–0.78 of a real row on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 0.90–0.93 on M3, and 1.44–1.65 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
  - Per operator (in-graph timing and kernel profiles), a padded row costs what a real one does in GEMMs past the ~280-row compute ridge (`q × n` rows, 384 at K=3 and 96 requests), norms and collectives; attention skips it.
  - Routed experts skip it only where the MoE reads `is_padding` (DeepSeek-V4's mega-MoE). The TRT-LLM monolithic MoE on M3 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next computes padded tokens.
  - On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 63% of the padded cost is one sparse-indexer kernel at ~87 µs per padded request: DeepGEMM's SM schedule puts every padded row on the last SM. Scheduling only the real rows, a separate fix outside this PR, brings DeepSeek-V4's padded/real cost from 1.44–1.51 to 0.54–0.57 (measured).
  - Under serving batch distributions this grid pads at most 0.6% of target time.
  - Denser grids (every count up to 64 then 32 per doubling, or every count) gain at most 0.3% end to end. Power-of-two grids lose 3–4.5% of engine time (3.0–6.5% tok/s).
- **Cost.**
  - Count: 112 target graphs take about 1.8 GiB of graph-exec memory and about 1 min of capture.
  - Width: the widest graph has `max_num_seqs × q` tokens. It costs about 0.8 GiB on M3 (K=3).

- **What is captured.** Decode batches mix query lengths under adaptive verification. - **Cost.** 11.2 MiB and 0.64 s per graph. The pool is set by the widest graph: on DeepSeek-V4.1 with 1024 × 6 tokens, about 12 GiB more than main.

- [ ] **T1. A size list and its cap must agree**, as main requires for the legacy pair. Raise when both are set and the cap differs from the list's max. Today a decode cap above the list's max is silently lowered, so adaptive verification follows the list while the docstring says it follows the cap. *Small; the next version of this PR.*
- [ ] **T2. Minimality cuts.** About 56 lines of docstrings and comments, and 25–30 lines of code, can go without changing behavior. A reviewer's list is ready. *Small; the next version of this PR.*
- [ ] **T3. Multi-token drafters (DSpark, DFlash, multi-module MTP) cover `max_num_seqs`**, with their shapes recorded in the max. *Depends on #59537 (one capture stream per device, aoshen02, draft).*
  - Without #59537, the widest draft graph needs its own memory: 2.7 GiB more at 1024 than at 512 requests on DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
  - Gain: 5–11% at DeepSeek-V4-Flash concurrency 1024 with the target at 512.
- [ ] **T4. Free the aux hidden states each PIECEWISE size keeps.** The change is ready on a branch, not yet proposed upstream: https://github.com/Pb314314/vllm/commit/9336eae65207e32b159e644a2b0c28ca3d9738fb. Breakable PIECEWISE graphs keep the drafter's aux hidden states alive per size, because `weak_ref_tensors` goes one level deep.
  - It costs 2.7–8 GiB on DeepSeek-V4, M3 and Kimi-K3.
  - The change is 12 lines plus a test, and gives KV +3.9% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and +4.4% on M3. *Separate PR; also on main.*
- [ ] **T5. Prefill cap 16K at DP = 1**, after T4. 8192 / 16384 engine time is 1.357 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash TEP 8K/1K. Under DP > 1 it stays 8192 until the gather-based DP/EP MoE skips padded rows: on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next DP4+EP, 8K is 14–20% faster.
- [ ] **T6. The CUDA graph memory estimate.**
  - Fix order: #59368 without its double count with #60186, then #62860, #61509, #57926 and #59537, then budgets for our persistent output buffers and for M3's and Kimi's workspaces.
  - Each fix is measured on its own. The combined stack has not run.
  - Most of this PR's DeepSeek KV gap comes from the estimate: see Differences from main.
- [ ] **T7. DeepSeek-V4 sparse-indexer padding.** DeepGEMM's SM schedule runs every padded decode row on the last SM.
  - Building the schedule over the real rows brings the padded/real cost from 1.44–1.51 to 0.54–0.57, with the same GSM8K. End to end it is −1 to −3% TPOT with this PR's decode grid.
  - *Separate PR.*
- [ ] **T8. A drafter cap separate from the target's.** The widest one-token draft graph holds the drafter's logits: +1.02 GiB for Gemma 4 E2B's 262k vocabulary.
- [ ] **T9. DSpark's request counts from its own q**, closing the K/(K+1) window off SM100. At concurrency 68 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash K=7 that window measured −4% / −10% (n = 2, not resolved).
- [ ] **T10. Open checks.**
  - DeepSeek-V4.1's decoder-replay bound follows the widest graph: about 32 replay sizes on GB200 against 8, roughly 0.5 GiB. This is estimated from code; measure it on GB200.
  - DeepSeek-V4.1's specialized-decode `metadata_graphs.capture_keys` still bounds its keys by `max_num_batched_tokens`. Under dynamic SD it can record keys that never run. GB300 only.
  - Dynamic-SD tiers capture only the request counts their schedule reaches. A uniform batch formed outside its tier would run PIECEWISE, where main ran FULL. Check with a scheduler trace under token-budget pressure.
- [ ] **T11. Coverage this cluster cannot run.**
  - H100/H200: off-SM100 graph sets were only emulated on GB200.
  - DFlash and multi-module MTP on GPU: no cached model pair.
  - Prefill context parallel, multi-node TP and LoRA end to end.
- [ ] **T12. Measure main with `max_cudagraph_capture_size=8192`** end to end, to replace the Overview's estimate of its graph cost.
- [ ] **T13. A fair KV comparison on DeepSeek.** Apply the estimate fixes to both main and this PR (#59368, #61509, #62860, and #60186 without its double count), then compare KV on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Expected, derived: V4.1 at or above main; V4 at about 0.85–0.9 of main, and about 1.0 with T14.
- [ ] **T14. DeepSeek's sparse-indexer decode logits.** Share one logits buffer between the decode graphs and the eager path, or compute the logits in request chunks on SM100, as #62169 does on SM90/SM120. That removes about 10 GiB per GPU at 1024 requests × 8 tokens. A separate PR.

## Not a duplicate

- #61882 refactors decode/mixed planning without a config change.
- #62209 adds an opt-in prefill subset of the shared list.
- #56136 and #62040 patch dynamic-SD and DSpark reachability. This PR covers both by construction, and their cases are in the tests.
- #60265 changes the default floor.
- None of them separates the two kinds' units and caps.
