items.title: [Perf][Attention] FlashInfer prefill for DiffKV attention on SM12x
items.body:
## Overview On SM12x (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, DGX Spark/GB10) there is no FA3/FA4, so DiffKV models (K/V head sizes differ; MiMo-V2: 192/128) run every attention step on `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV`. This PR adds `TRITON_FLASHINFER_DIFFKV`, built with the existing `create_composite_attention_backend`. It routes batches that contain a prefill on plain causal full-attention layers to FlashInfer's paged prefill (`head_dim_vo`), using the same packed cache. Decode-only and verification-only batches, and all CUDA graph capture and replay, stay on `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV`. Related: - #58177 and #59673 optimize the Triton DiffKV kernel. They are complementary and are benchmarked against below. - #59052 pins Triton DiffKV to `UNIFORM_BATCH` CUDA graphs, the same support level this composite reports. - #46963 also uses FlashInfer prefill on SM12x. ## Claims All on DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), MiMo-V2.6-Flash. - **Prefill attention, one full-attention layer at TP2,** vs Triton DiffKV with #58177 + #59673 applied. Cold-L2 CUDA-graph timing; `plan()` host time is reported separately below. - 2.27–2.29× for 512+-token chunks over a 32K prefix; - 2.17× for a fresh 8K chunk, 1.84× fresh 2K, 1.24× fresh 512; - 3.07× for 64 tokens and 6.41× for 17 tokens over a 32K prefix; - slower for fresh chunks of ≤64 tokens: 0.45–0.83×, i.e. 1.2–3.6 µs per layer. - **End to end on the PR base** (main `18c19eaf2` with and without this PR): cold-prefill TTFT at 96K tokens goes from 72.3 s to 40.6 s (**1.78×**); 1.46× at 48K, 1.23× at 24K. - Single-request decode is unchanged. - Fresh 23–34-token prompts are 2–6 ms slower at p50 (1–4%); 66–515-token prompts are 4–10 ms faster. - **Accuracy:** no observed degradation in gsm8k or full-vocabulary logprobs. - **Cost:** on this configuration the KV cache is 0.59 GiB smaller (6.6% fewer tokens), mostly from FlashInfer's workspace (details below). - **Off switch:** `VLLM_DIFFKV_FLASHINFER_PREFILL=0` restores `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV` for every layer. - **SM120** (RTX PRO 6000, confirmed by @waynehacking8): tests pass, and FlashInfer is 2.5–28× faster than Triton main for every chunk over a cached prefix and 2.6–3.1× for fresh chunks of 2K+. Fresh chunks up to 512 tokens are 0.43–0.98×, so the fresh-prompt crossover is later than on GB10. ## Validation **Not a duplicate.** I searched open and closed PRs for `diffkv flashinfer`, `DiffKV FlashInfer prefill`, `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV`, `diffkv sm120` and `MiMo FlashInfer prefill`. None route DiffKV attention to FlashInfer. ### Environments The hardware is GB10 throughout, except the SM120 check below, which @waynehacking8 ran on an RTX PRO 6000 ([comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61178#issuecomment-6258374504), [gist](https://gist.github.com/waynehacking8/fe4b2d3280ff52f2c21f184de3b10ef7)). | label | vLLM | FlashInfer | used for | |---|---|---|---| | **PR base** | main `18c19eaf2` precompiled cu130 aarch64 wheel; "+PR" adds this PR's Python files (the PR changes no compiled code) | 0.7.0.post1 (main's pin) | tests, layer timing, end-to-end A/B, short-prompt TTFT | | **rebased** | this PR as `c379d3fab` on main `74f4404f5`, run from the main `fe4df3df0` wheel (one unrelated commit earlier) + this PR's files | 0.7.0.post1 | tests, serving re-check | | **old base** | `7f1a539` + this change (plus a local `max_decode_query_len` shim) | 0.6.18.post1 | gsm8k, logprobs, mixed load | - **Shared stack:** torch 2.13.0+cu130 and triton 3.7.1. The MoE backend is b12x 1.5.0, which needs `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` 4.7.1 (main pins 4.8.0); this only affects the MoE path. - **Model:** `XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-MOPD` @ `2479e2d0029e`. - **Server:** ```bash vllm serve MiMo-V2.6-Flash-MOPD --tensor-parallel-size 2 --nnodes 2 \ --distributed-executor-backend mp --gpu-memory-utilization 0.87 \ --max-model-len 300000 --max-num-seqs 16 --moe-backend b12x \ --no-async-scheduling --trust-remote-code --generation-config vllm \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"MiMo-V2.6-Flash-MOPD/dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7}' ``` - **Video profiling:** on the PR base both arms also pass `--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"video": 0}'`. Main's encoder profiling with a maximum-size video exhausted GB10's unified memory during startup and hung the GPU driver, independent of this PR. All workloads below are text-only. - **Rebase:** #57169 removed `set_kernel_block_size()` from the metadata builder base class; the builder now takes its page size from `kv_cache_spec.block_size`, as other builders on main do. - **Memory on the rebased base:** at `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.87`, main `fe4df3df0` + PR sized the KV cache at 20.05 GiB, compared with 18.42 GiB for `18c19eaf2` + PR with the same flags. Host MemAvailable then fell below 3 GB during startup warmup, and my watchdog stopped the server. The re-check therefore ran at 0.85. I did not measure main without this PR on this base, so the cause of the larger KV cache is not isolated. ### Tests ```bash pytest -v tests/kernels/attention/test_flashinfer_diffkv_prefill.py ``` | environment | result | |---|---| | rebased (main `fe4df3df0` + PR), FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1 | **99 passed** | | PR base (+PR), FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1 | **99 passed** | | old base, FlashInfer 0.6.18.post1 | 98 passed, 1 failed | The old-base failure is `test_layer_eligibility[kwargs3]` (FP8 KV), which needs #58128 (on main). **Numerics.** The backend's own plan/run is checked against an FP32 PyTorch reference, because the existing DiffKV test needs FA3/FA4 and skips on SM12x. - Inputs: - a scattered block table; - physical layouts HND / NHD, each with and without layer interleaving; - block sizes 16 and 64; - a fresh 2K prompt, 2K over an 8K prefix, 256 over a 32K prefix, and 17 over an 8K prefix; - a mixed batch with decode rows. - Checks: `assert_close(atol=rtol=2e-2)` and relative L2 < 1e-2. - An FP16 subset covers both layouts. **Behavior** tests check: - auto-selection and its fallbacks: sinks, sliding window, FP8 KV, unvalidated head sizes, and the opt-out variable; - per-layer eligibility on real impls; - `host_seq_lens` for pure-prefill (no readback) and mixed speculative batches (exact lengths); - that the capture variant is Triton for uniform batches up to `1 + num_speculative_tokens`. **GPU sync.** Repeated pure-prefill and mixed speculative plan+run steps pass after warmup under `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`, via `enable_gpu_sync_check` and `with_gpu_sync_check`. With pinned staging disabled, the checker raises on the unpinned non-blocking copy. (Old base, both FlashInfer versions.) **CI coverage.** Buildkite has no SM12x runner, so the GPU cases skip in CI. ### Layer timing (PR base) ```bash python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_flashinfer_diffkv_prefill.py --method cudagraph \ --block-sizes 64 --chunk 17 64 512 2048 8192 --prefix 0 32768 ``` - MiMo-V2.6-Flash full-attention layer, TP2 (32 q / 2 KV heads, K192/V128, BF16), one request, block size 64. - Median of FlashInfer's `bench_gpu_time_with_cudagraph` with `cold_l2_cache=True`. Inputs are preallocated and passed through the timer, so it rotates them. CUPTI was unavailable. - Triton+PRs is main's kernel with #58177 @ `2e41b30` and #59673 @ `9103f7d` applied; their outputs are bit-identical to main's. | chunk | prefix | Triton main (µs) | Triton+PRs (µs) | this PR (µs) | vs Triton+PRs | vs main | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 17 | 0 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 6.6 | 0.45× | 0.45× | | 17 | 32K | 1,399 | 1,446 | 225 | 6.41× | 6.23× | | 64 | 0 | 7.7 | 6.1 | 7.3 | 0.83× | 1.06× | | 64 | 32K | 3,108 | 1,737 | 566 | 3.07× | 5.50× | | 512 | 0 | 153 | 102 | 83 | 1.24× | 1.85× | | 512 | 32K | 17,435 | 10,979 | 4,846 | 2.27× | 3.60× | | 2K | 0 | 2,092 | 1,211 | 660 | 1.84× | 3.20× | | 2K | 32K | 70,411 | 41,449 | 18,291 | 2.27× | 3.86× | | 8K | 0 | 34,095 | 19,443 | 8,964 | 2.17× | 3.78× | | 8K | 32K | 314,982 | 180,821 | 79,054 | 2.29× | 3.96× | - Relative L2 against Triton is 6.6e-4 to 3.9e-3. - Warm-L2 timing (same buffers repeated) gave the same speedups within 3%, except fresh 512 (1.47× warm vs 1.24× cold). **Per-step costs added by the FlashInfer path,** reported separately because host planning can overlap GPU work: - Kernel: 1.2–3.6 µs slower per layer for fresh chunks of ≤64 tokens, about 11–32 µs per step over MiMo's 9 full-attention layers. Faster for every other measured shape. - `plan()`: 101–134 µs host time per step that routes to FlashInfer (median of 20 calls), shared by all layers. One outlier: 548 µs for the fresh 17-token case in the Triton+PRs run. That was the first case in its process (after one untimed `plan()` call), and the identical case measured 104 µs in the Triton-main run. A warmup effect is likely, but I did not verify it, so it is reported here rather than excluded (raw log: `results_v8_bench_coldl2_triton_prs.txt`). - Serving impact, measured directly in the short-prompt table below. ### SM120 (RTX PRO 6000, run by @waynehacking8) From [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61178#issuecomment-6258374504); runs, crossover sweep and job log in [the gist](https://gist.github.com/waynehacking8/fe4b2d3280ff52f2c21f184de3b10ef7). - Environment: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, this PR on main `153a17166e`, FlashInfer 0.7.2. The Triton DiffKV kernel file is identical to main's. - Tests: 99 passed, none skipped. - Layer timing: the benchmark above with `--method cudagraph` and its defaults, two runs (they agree within 4%), block sizes 16 and 64. Speedup is against Triton main. | chunk | prefix 0 | prefix 2K | prefix 8K | prefix 32K | |---|---|---|---|---| | 8 | 0.43–0.46× | 5.2–5.6× | 17.6–18.7× | 27.7–28.3× | | 17 | 0.43–0.46× | 4.9–5.3× | 8.4–8.7× | 15.4–16.4× | | 64 | 0.61–0.63× | 2.5–2.7× | 4.4–4.6× | 6.2–6.8× | | 512 | 0.95–0.98× | | 2.7–2.8× | 2.9× | | 2K | 2.6–2.7× | | 3.1–3.2× | 3.2× | | 8K | 3.1× | | 3.2–3.3× | 3.3× | - Over a cached prefix FlashInfer is faster from 8 tokens up. For fresh chunks the crossover is between 512 and 2K tokens, against about 64 on GB10, so fresh 17–512-token chunks routed by the 16-token floor are slower by at most about 4 µs per full-attention layer (6.9 vs 3.2 µs at 17 tokens). - `plan()`: 156–201 µs host time per step (101–134 µs on GB10), not included in the timings. - Relative L2 against the FP32 reference is 6.6e-4 to 3.9e-3. ### End to end on the PR base (main ± PR) Single request, cache-cold prompts. | prompt tokens | main TTFT | main + PR TTFT | speedup | |---|---|---|---| | 1.5K | 0.78 s | 0.75 s | 1.04× | | 6K | 2.17 s | 1.96 s | 1.11× | | 24K | 9.95 s | 8.12 s | 1.23× | | 48K | 25.33 s | 17.40 s | 1.46× | | 96K | 72.31 s | 40.59 s | 1.78× | - **Decode** (2048 tokens, DFlash k=7): main 55.9 / 53.7 (code) and 29.0 / 27.9 (prose) tok/s; main + PR 54.4 / 53.4 and 29.2 / 28.1 tok/s. - **Engine logs:** - main + PR selects `TRITON_FLASHINFER_DIFFKV` for full-attention layers and `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV` for SWA layers, on Model Runner V2. - Both arms captured full decode and DFlash CUDA graphs. - Chat and tool-call smoke requests succeeded on both. - **Old base** (`7f1a539` ± this change): the same TTFT pattern, 96K 72.8 s → 40.6 s. **Short cache-cold prompts.** One request at a time, 30 requests per size, `max_tokens=1`, after warmup; one server start per arm. | prompt tokens | main p50 / p90 | main + PR p50 / p90 | Δ p50 | |---|---|---|---| | 23 | 173.0 / 185.5 ms | 179.5 / 187.5 ms | +6.5 ms | | 34 | 198.3 / 211.7 ms | 200.6 / 214.4 ms | +2.3 ms | | 66 | 228.3 / 235.7 ms | 224.1 / 235.3 ms | −4.2 ms | | 129 | 266.5 / 286.1 ms | 256.0 / 276.7 ms | −10.5 ms | | 515 | 296.9 / 301.3 ms | 291.2 / 296.6 ms | −5.7 ms | ### Re-check after rebase (main `fe4df3df0` + PR, 0.85) One server start, PR arm only. There is no main arm on this base, so the speedups above come from the PR base. - The engine log selects `TRITON_FLASHINFER_DIFFKV` for full-attention layers and `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV` for SWA layers. Chat and tool-call smoke requests succeeded. - Cold-prefill TTFT: 1.5K 0.74 s, 6K 1.98 s, 24K 8.33 s, 48K 17.44 s, 96K 41.25 s (PR base: 0.75, 1.96, 8.12, 17.40, 40.59 s). - Decode: 53.8 / 49.3 (code) and 28.0 / 26.9 (prose) tok/s. - Short prompts, p50: 23 tokens 178.2 ms, 34 207.9 ms, 66 225.5 ms, 129 265.7 ms, 515 299.2 ms. ### Concurrent generation with arriving prompts (old base) - Workload: 8 streams generating up to 600 tokens (DFlash k=7, temperature 0). - Phase A has no arrivals. Phase B adds a cache-cold 8K-token prompt every 6 s, so prefill shares batches with decode/verify rows. - One run per arm. - **The arms got different random arrival prompts of the same length.** The workload seeded with `hash()`, which is randomized per process; the script now uses a fixed seed. | phase | metric | base | this PR | |---|---|---|---| | decode only | stream tok/s | 127.8 | 124.3 | | decode only | chunk gap p50 / p99 | 249 / 316 ms | 250 / 329 ms | | with arrivals | stream tok/s | 88.8 | 92.7 | | with arrivals | chunk gap p50 / p90 / p99 | 262 / 775 / 846 ms | 260 / 741 / 759 ms | | with arrivals | arrival TTFT mean / p90 | 3.76 / 3.86 s | 3.50 / 3.64 s | No regression was observed in one synchronous-scheduling run (`--no-async-scheduling`). The decode-only phase runs identical code, which suggests about ±3% noise. Async scheduling is not measured. ### gsm8k (old base) ```bash python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000 --use-chat-completions \ --max-tokens 1024 --temperature 0 --max-concurrency 32 \ --request-timeout-seconds 14400 --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}' ``` 1319 questions, 5-shot, chat, thinking off; two runs each. | config | run 1 | run 2 | invalid | |---|---|---|---| | base (`TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV`) | 0.963 | 0.961 | 0.0% | | this PR | 0.961 | 0.964 | 0.0% | The longer timeout is needed because the evaluator starts all 1319 requests at once behind a connection limit. Each request's `aiohttp` timeout includes time spent waiting for a connection, so queued requests expired at the 600 s default.
Full-vocabulary logprobs vs base (old base) These are `prompt_logprobs` on a fixed text set, compared token by token. The noise column is two runs of one fixed configuration against each other. | text | tokens | mean \|Δ logprob\| | ppl ratio | top-1 agree | noise \|Δ\| / ppl | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | code (agent) | 1785 | 0.0941 | 0.997 | 97.4% | 0.0896 / 1.001 | | code (site) | 1931 | 0.0573 | 0.997 | 98.0% | 0.0518 / 0.996 | | prose | 529 | 0.0194 | 1.002 | 100.0% | 0.0246 / 1.011 | | json | 2330 | 0.0045 | 1.002 | 100.0% | 0.0041 / 1.002 | | math | 1376 | 0.0054 | 0.999 | 99.9% | 0.0068 / 0.999 | | tool call | 303 | 0.8095 | 1.211 | 98.7% | 0.7744 / 0.982 | The tool-call sample is short and high-entropy (mean NLL 4.3). Its perplexity ratio swings by about ±20% even between two runs of the identical FlashInfer kernel (1.246).
Raw results, logs and scripts: https://gist.github.com/siddharth1825/7e3c542800bef7f7ee6c03f6ba80487c ## Details ### Selection `MiMoV2Attention` keeps its order: FA DiffKV when FA3/FA4 is usable, then `TRITON_FLASHINFER_DIFFKV`, then `TRITON_ATTN_DIFFKV`. The new backend is auto-selected only when all of these hold: - CUDA, compute capability 12.x, FlashInfer present; - full attention: no sliding window, no sinks; - FP16/BF16 compute with a 16-bit KV cache; - head sizes (192, 128), the only pair tested. It is also selectable with `--attention-backend TRITON_FLASHINFER_DIFFKV`. ### Routing - FlashInfer when the batch's longest query exceeds `max(16, max_decode_query_len)`; Triton otherwise, and for image-prefix batches. - Decode or verify rows that share a batch with a prefill run on FlashInfer with it. - `capture_variant = 0`. The threshold is never below the uniform decode/verify width, so CUDA graph replay always selects Triton. - A KV cache group containing any layer FlashInfer does not cover (window, sinks, ALiBi, soft-cap, FP8 KV) always uses Triton. - The 16-token floor is not tuned for fresh prompts. Over a cached prefix, FlashInfer wins from 17 tokens; fresh prompts break even around 64 tokens. ### Metadata - `plan()` runs once per step in the builder, shared by every layer in the group. - As in `FlashInferMetadataBuilder.build`, the query offsets, page offsets, last-page lengths and an explicit `seq_lens` are staged in pinned memory, so `plan()`'s non-blocking copies stay asynchronous. - The builder reuses `_copy_page_indices_kernel` and joins the composite's workspace sharing. ### Host sequence lengths - `seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound` is exact for prefill rows, and for all rows without speculative decoding, so those batches never read back from the GPU. - A batch with a row that may be a spec-decode row (query length ≤ `max_decode_query_len`) reads exact `seq_lens` back inside `gpu_sync_allowed()`. That row's upper bound assumes every draft was accepted, and FlashInfer needs exact lengths. - Without async scheduling the bound is often exact too. That is not used, because MRV2 adaptive verification also makes per-row token counts an upper bound. ### Cache and FlashInfer path - The FlashInfer child subclasses the Triton DiffKV backend, so both share one cache spec and tensor. K/V are passed as last-dim strided views of the packed cache, in HND or NHD physical layout, with or without layer interleaving. - The call is `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper(workspace, "HND")` with `plan(..., head_dim_vo=128, causal=True, seq_lens=...)`; the wrapper resolves to the `fa2` backend on SM12x. - The SM120 fused 192×128 kernels reported unreachable in the 0.6.18/0.7.0 wrappers are not used. - **JIT build on 0.7.0.post1.** The aarch64 `flashinfer-jit-cache` wheel is a stub that depends on per-architecture packages vLLM does not install, so the 192/128 module is JIT-built on first use: 19 s in isolation. In serving it completes during startup; the first long prompt after a restart was not measurably slower. ### Memory - **Workspace.** It is sized like the FlashInfer backend's: `max(VLLM_FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BUFFER_SIZE, tokens × heads × head_dim × 16)`. With this config's 2048-token budget, that resolves to the 394 MB default. - **KV cache.** On the PR base, KV cache memory went from 19.01 to 18.42 GiB (1,428,918 → 1,335,006 tokens). - **Possible follow-up.** A smaller floor for this prefill-only use could recover most of it. It is not changed here: FlashInfer errors rather than grows when the workspace is too small, and the default is the same one the FlashInfer backend uses. ### Why decode and CUDA graphs stay on Triton - Decode is bandwidth-bound with short queries. Triton DiffKV already has 2D/3D split-KV paths for it, and measured decode was unchanged. - Only Triton is captured. Moving decode/verify-only batches to FlashInfer needs a graph-safe DiffKV decode/verify plan (persistent buffers, `fast_plan`), which is a separate change. - **Cost.** The composite reports `UNIFORM_BATCH` instead of `ALWAYS`. - Under the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, uniform decode still runs as full graphs, and mixed batches already ran piecewise. - Only `cudagraph_mode=FULL` with mixed batches loses full graphs on these layers. ### Complexity About 460 new lines in one new backend file, plus small edits: - selection: 18 lines in `mimo_v2.py`; - the env var; - the registry entry; - docs. There are no changes to the model runner, scheduler, KV cache manager or the Triton kernel. ### AI assistance Claude (Anthropic) was used to write the change, run the tests and benchmarks on our DGX Sparks, and draft this description. I reviewed every changed line and the validation results. cc @mgoin: SM12x + FlashInfer prefill, related to #46963. ---

items.title: [New Model][Nvidia] Add SM12x support for DeepSeek V4 Flash with essential fixes
items.body: ## Summary This PR enables DeepSeek V4 Flash on SM120/SM121 Blackwell client hardware by carrying the SM12x fallback and tuning stack needed for the current vLLM V1 path. It targets RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, RTX 5090-class SM120, and GB10 / DGX Spark SM121 users who cannot use SM100-only TMEM / `tcgen05` kernels. The branch is **reconciled on top of the merged #43477** and provides the **stock-deps path**: DeepSeek V4 on SM120/121 that builds and serves on *released* FlashInfer / DeepGEMM wheels, complementing #43477's route that needs the unreleased FlashInfer #3395 + DeepGEMM #324 dependency branches. It is kept **synced onto current `upstream/main`**. **Latest validated head: tag `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260809` (`aa0d513027`), synced onto `upstream/main` as of 2026-08-09 (`f18e10a7e1`)** — see [Update 2026-08-09](#update-2026-08-09) below. **The default model runner is now V2**; `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` still selects V1, which stays supported. **Model / speculative-decode status.** `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` is the checkpoint this branch is validated on. It **removed the MTP heads** and folded the DSpark draft into the main checkpoint, so **DSpark (`method: "dspark"`, `num_speculative_tokens: 5`) is the speculative path**; MTP is supported only for older checkpoints that still carry those weights. Running without speculation is also fully supported and validated. ## Change footprint — model kernels vs. core-vLLM touch points 187 files, ~+29.1k / −1.3k against `upstream/main`, of which ~10.7k added lines are tests. The branch splits cleanly into model/kernel code and a small set of core-vLLM integration points: - **DeepSeek-V4 model + SM12x kernels — the enablement itself.** Everything under `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/**` plus the SM12x sparse-MLA decode / indexer / DeepGEMM kernels that live in shared dirs (`v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_mla_kernels.py`, `model_executor/layers/sparse_attn_indexer.py`, `v1/attention/backends/mla/{indexer,sparse_swa}.py`, `utils/deep_gemm.py`, `kernels/mhc/tilelang.py`), the new DSv4 reasoning parser / tokenizer, and device tuning JSONs. - **C128A metadata device→host sync removed** (`models/deepseek_v4/sparse_mla.py`, perf) — `_c128a_effective_topk_width` takes the max position from the CPU-side `CommonAttentionMetadata.max_seq_len` instead of a per-step `int(positions.max().item())` device sync, dropping a launch-stream stall on every C128A metadata step. On a fully-masked row — every candidate `-inf`, which structured-output constraints can produce — *no* block has an active lane, so every block stores the filler and the reduce kernel returns it verbatim as the sampled token. Nothing downstream bounded it: the runner clamped `input_ids` with `min=0` only, and the DSv4 hash-MoE router indexes `tid2eid[token_id * 6 + lane]` on a `[vocab_size, 6]` table. Result is an illegal memory access on every TP rank. This is the producer on the **V1** path, which is this branch's default. @alexbi29's report traced the same class of defect to the V2 samplers (#50843) — a real defect, but a different tree. Fixed by folding out-of-range to `0` (matching `torch.argmax` on such a row, so the fused kernel stays bit-identical to the eager reference) and making the runner clamp two-sided. Worth stating plainly for anyone with similar gates: **our own gates could not have caught this**. The fused path is skipped when `all_greedy`, and both our long-context recall gate and GSM8K are greedy, so they are structurally incapable of executing that kernel. The new regression test is explicitly non-greedy. - **Adopted #50844** (`3df857ba50`) — bound `token_id` before the `tid2eid` gather. Defence in depth; `prompt_token_ids` reach that gather directly when `--skip-tokenizer-init` disables the engine's vocab check. **Not** taking #50843 (V2-tree only, inert on our default) or #50845, which has a defect reported on its own thread. - **Eager scratch pool is now OFF by default** (`d42b8d9f55`, `b1ef3033f4`), opt-in via `VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_EAGER_SCRATCH_POOL=1`. @tobymao bisected output corruption under concurrent mixed prefill+decode to it: pool active 7/7 rounds corrupt, disabled 0/2. Their diagnosis is the useful part: the pre-pool code was race-free *for free* because per-call transients go through the caching allocator, whose cross-stream reuse is event-guarded — the pool reuses memory without that machinery, so no static partitioning fixes it. Making the cross-layer reuse safe needs producer-waits-on-consumer events against the real stream graph; until then, off by default. - **Two contributor PRs merged** — jasl/vllm#37 (tuned FP8 W8A8 config for `N=4096,K=12288` on RTX PRO 6000) and jasl/vllm#38 (hoist the E8M0 block-scale upcast out of the FP8 GEMM hot path, 13,561 kernel launches removed per 25 decode steps), both from @alexbi29. - **`num_speculative_tokens` rule relaxed.** Upstream removed its own assertion in #50869 as "invalid". A request admitted later in the same step can match those hashes and read unwritten values. `MambaManager` has guarded this since #29387; no other manager does. This is **vllm-project/vllm#42359**, open and unmerged. Two more reports look like the same triple on different models — **#50188** (prefix caching + MTP spec decode + fp8 KV, byte-identical repeat requests, RTX 5090 / Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4) and **#43559** (closed without a merged fix). Anyone on `--enable-prefix-caching` with speculative decoding is exposed; DeepSeek-V4 is not special here. What makes it hard to catch: **the damage persists**. A serve that loses the race keeps serving from the poisoned blocks for its lifetime, so a later *serial* request fails too — which is why it looked like a per-serve "mode" rather than a race. It is also stochastic, roughly half of cold serves. ### Evidence Same binary, `VLLM_ALLOW_SPEC_DEC_SAME_STEP_PREFIX_HIT` the only variable, cache populated by the real gate, **4 fresh serves per arm** (a single clean serve proves nothing at ~50% incidence), 3 arthur c=12 runs each: | | serve 1 | serve 2 | serve 3 | serve 4 | mean | min | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | guard **off** | 22/23/24 | **6/5/3** | **14/9/10** | **7/8/7** | 11.5 | 3 | | guard **on** | 23/22/21 | 20/22/20 | 22/23/23 | 23/22/23 | 22.0 | 20 | Mann-Whitney U, p = 0.0043. Every serve's runner and guard state was read back from the serve log rather than assumed. **It also fixes V1**, which was not expected: V1's arthur c=12 goes 20.7 → 23.0 with the guard on (24.0 with prefix caching disabled entirely). V1's own 2–4 needle shortfall was the same defect, not an inherent concurrency margin. ### Runner arbitration, re-run on the fixed tree Same tree, same guard mode, **runner the only variable**: | | V1 | V2 | | --- | --- | --- | | arthur c=12, 4 serves × 3 | 22.3 / 21.7 / 21.7 / 21.0 → **21.67** | 22.0 / 20.7 / 22.7 / 22.7 → **22.00** | | pp2048 d8192 / 16384 / 32768 | 1427 / 1363 / 1216 | **1472 / 1421 / 1303** (+3.1% / +4.2% / +7.1%) | | tg128 mean | 39.95 / 41.16 / 35.25 | **41.56 / 49.61 / 45.18** | | e2e TTFT | 1437 / 1506 / 1689 ms | **1393 / 1444 / 1576 ms** | | GPU KV cache | 339,194 tok | **423,752 tok** (+24.9%) | | GSM8K strict / flexible | 0.9378 / 0.9401 | 0.9401 / 0.9439 | | issue19 · multi-needle · c=1 | PASS · 48/48, 0 leaks · 2/2 | PASS · 48/48, 0 leaks · 2/2 | Recall: p = 0.697, neither side with a single-digit serve. GSM8K differs by <0.4 pp against ~1.1 pp single-run noise. **V2 is not behind anywhere and leads on throughput, latency and KV headroom, so it becomes the default.** `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` still selects V1, which stays supported. **Correction:** the *"V2 +6.6% draft acceptance"* figure in Update 2026-08-04 does **not** survive re-measurement — 2.772 (V1) vs 2.710 (V2) on the same formula and sample size, i.e. a tie. It was measured while V2 was poisoned. ### If you are running this branch **Nothing to set — the guard is on by default where it matters.** `KVCacheCoordinator` enables it whenever prefix caching and speculative decoding are both active, which is the only configuration in which a block hash can be published before its KV is written *and* a second request admitted in the same step to match it. This correction matters: an earlier revision of this update shipped V2 as the default while leaving the guard off by default, which would have handed a plain serve the exact combination measured at mean 11.5 with a 3/24 floor. Both changes looked like improvements in isolation. If you pulled `c054feedac`, take `aa0d513027` instead, or set the variable yourself. To turn it **off** (it is a real escape hatch, pinned by a test): ```bash VLLM_ALLOW_SPEC_DEC_SAME_STEP_PREFIX_HIT=0 ``` `1` is upstream's semantics, gated on `use_eagle`; on DeepSeek-V4 that covers only **2 of 5** managers and leaves the main MLA path unguarded — measured, not assumed, via a startup log line this branch adds that reports how many managers are actually guarded. `2` covers every group and is what the engine selects. Regression sweep on the merged tree: 261 passed, 1 failed, that one failing identically on the pre-merge tree `4ebd1fb698`. ### The two endpoints disagreed about the same model, twice `ResponsesRequest.reasoning` took its type from the OpenAI SDK, whose `ReasoningEffort` stops at `xhigh`, so DeepSeek's documented top tier `max` was rejected by schema validation on `/v1/responses` while `/v1/chat/completions` accepted it. Worse, and on the default path: with no thinking kwarg, `DeepSeekV4Tokenizer.apply_chat_template` defaults thinking **on** while `DeepSeekV4ReasoningParser` defaults it **off** and selects `IdentityReasoningParser`. The model reasoned and its reasoning, with a bare ``, came back inside `output_text` as though it were the answer — whenever a request omitted `reasoning`, which is exactly what a stock OpenAI SDK sends. Chat was immune only because it normalises thinking state at the protocol boundary, and its own docstring says why: *"so the tokenizer and reasoning parser see the same effective state"*. Responses never called that hook. The derivation now lives in `deepseek_v4_chat_kwargs` and both request types call it, so a third endpoint cannot repeat it. Measured on both checkpoints with no workaround flag set, 21/21 each: | | `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` | `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` | | --- | --- | --- | | silence: reasoning in its own field | PASS | PASS | | silence: no `` in the answer | PASS | PASS | | `effort: none` disables thinking | PASS | PASS | | six spellings × two endpoints | PASS | PASS | | `high` reasons deeper than `low` | +85% / +110% | +19% / +35% | 26 unit cases accompany it, 11 of which fail on the unpatched tree. `tests/reasoning` 440 passed, `tests/tokenizers_/test_deepseek_v4.py` 45 passed. ### Acceptance on the exact published SHA Everything above was re-measured on `d44e224ab9` — the commit this tag points at, after a second upstream sync (17 further commits, FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3) — not on an ancestor assumed to be equivalent. 17 of 18 checks pass: | check | result | | --- | --- | | four nodes clean at the SHA, FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3 | PASS | | `tests/v1/core` | 509 passed, 1 pre-existing failure | | default serve with **nothing set**: boots, runner V2, guard 5/5, no NameError | PASS | | arthur c=12 ×3 / c=1 | 22 / 20 / 23 · 2/2 | | GSM8K strict · issue19 · multi-needle | 0.9363 · PASS · 48/48, 0 leaks | | pp2048 d8192 | 1480.77 (arbitration V2 arm 1471.8) | | `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` → V1, guard still 5/5, c=1 2/2 | PASS | | `VLLM_ALLOW_SPEC_DEC_SAME_STEP_PREFIX_HIT=0` → guard 0/5, c=1 2/2 | PASS | **The one non-pass, and what it turned out to be.** `tests/v1/spec_decode` does not complete on this hardware — it wedges under a 30-minute bound on this head and on `4ebd1fb698` alike. Narrowed to `test_max_len.py` and measured both ways: | how it is run | result | | --- | --- | | whole file, one pytest process | wedges after ~7 min, 5 of 11 done | | each case in its own process | **11 of 11 pass**, free memory steady at 117 GiB | No individual case is broken. Each stands up a full engine, and repeated create/tear-down inside one process does not release resources fast enough on a **single-GPU** unified-memory node. That also explains why both trees wedge and why they stop at different points. It remains **unverified coverage rather than a pass**; running one process per case produces a verdict instead of a hang. `test_async_scheduling_pp_allows_rescheduling_with_output_placeholders` is the same class: it builds `pipeline_parallel_size=2`, and a GB10 node has one GPU, so it fails at config construction. It is the only case in `tests/v1/core` that needs more than one GPU; the other 509 pass. ### What this arbitration does and does not cover Everything above was measured on **one configuration**: 2-node TP=2, `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, DSpark `num_speculative_tokens: 5`, fp8 KV, `max_model_len` 131072, prefix caching on, GB10 (SM121). The default now applies to **every** DSpark config, including shapes not measured here — TP=4, other context lengths, the NVFP4 checkpoint, single-node setups. The reasoning generalises better than the numbers do: the race is in block publication and is not specific to a model shape, and V2's advantage comes from KV headroom and scheduling rather than anything config-specific. But if you run a materially different shape and see something worse, `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` returns you to V1 and a report would be welcome — that is a gap in our coverage, not a claim we have ruled out. ## Running DSpark DSpark is DeepSeek's self-drafting speculative-decode variant; on `0731` the draft weights are carried in the main checkpoint, so no separate `--speculative-model` is needed. ```bash vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \ --trust-remote-code \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 256 \ --max-model-len 49152 \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' ``` - `num_speculative_tokens` **must equal** the checkpoint's `dspark_block_size` (5). Larger values are rejected: they are never accepted and only waste draft compute. - `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` is mandatory — DSv4's `fp8_ds_mla` attention asserts an fp8 KV layout, so the default `auto` fails at model construction. Not DSpark-specific. - Runs on the **V1 runner by default** (correct long-context recall). `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` opts into the V2 DSpark speculator; V2's long-context recall is correct after the jasl/vllm#26 padded-Q fix. - If you measure draft acceptance yourself, **use prose**. On counting or repeated text the Markov head alone reaches 68–100% acceptance even with the neural draft path degraded, which hides real regressions entirely. ## Dependencies (stock-deps path) Pins on the current head: torch 2.13.0 (triton 3.7.1) · `flashinfer-python` / `flashinfer-cubin` 0.6.15.post1 · tilelang 0.1.12 · `nvidia-cutlass-dsl[cu13]` 4.6.0 · `quack-kernels>=0.6.1` · nvidia-nccl-cu13 2.30.7 (multi-node, see below). - **FlashInfer** is pinned in `requirements/cuda.txt` (`flashinfer-python` **and** the GitHub-release `flashinfer-cubin`, which must be the same version); it ships the SM120 packed sparse-MLA kernels, so a stock build picks them up with no manual install dance. - **GB10 / multi-node**: pin `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7` on every node. A rebuild silently reverts it to torch's bundled version, and a per-node mismatch hangs the NCCL handshake. - The SM120 **decode** (`VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_FLASHINFER_SM120_DECODE`) and **prefill** (`VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_FLASHINFER_SM120_PREFILL`) FlashInfer sparse-MLA paths **default on**; set either `=0` to fall back to the FlashMLA / Triton path. Both are availability-gated, so stock installs without the kernel degrade gracefully rather than raising. ## Running the NVFP4 checkpoint This branch also serves `nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4` on SM12x (RTX PRO 6000 / GB10). The NVFP4 MoE auto-selects the FlashInfer CUTLASS backend (the SwiGLU-clamp model gate accepts it), so no `--moe-backend` flag and no special FlashInfer build are required: ```bash vllm serve nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4 \ --trust-remote-code --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 ``` Expert-parallel off (plain TP) is the supported path. Accuracy matches MXFP4 (GSM8K 8-shot ~0.96 on both SM120 and SM121). On SM12x NVFP4 is **not** a memory or throughput win versus MXFP4: NVFP4 weights are ~4 GiB/GPU larger, leaving less KV-cache room; single-stream prefill is marginally faster and aggregate decode marginally slower. Its value here is checkpoint availability / parity with the SM100 datacenter path — MXFP4 remains the better practical choice on consumer Blackwell. ## AI assistance disclosure AI assistants, including OpenAI Codex/GPT models and Anthropic Claude models, were used for code review, refactoring support, regression-script writing, and benchmark analysis. The branch was validated through human review plus the commands and harness artifacts listed above; every performance and accuracy number quoted was measured on real SM120/SM121 hardware.

items.title: [MoE][Offload] Run MoE models exceeding VRAM via expert CPU offloading with GPU cache (--moe-expert-cache-size)
items.body:
## Purpose

`CachedWeightProvider` — MoE expert CPU offloading with GPU LFRU cache, addressing [RFC #38256](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38256).

Expert weights live in CPU pinned memory; a fixed-size GPU cache holds the hottest N experts per layer using LFRU (frequency-weighted LRU) eviction. LFRU prevents early layers from monopolizing the cache — a known problem with pure LRU in sequential MoE execution. Models that exceed GPU VRAM can now run on smaller hardware.

**No runner bypass** — all paths go through `quant_method.apply()`. EP dispatch, DP chunking, and shared expert overlap work unchanged.

**References:** [RFC #38256](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38256) | [tinyserve](https://github.com/e1n00r/tinyserve) (production validation, 481 tests)

## Test results

**Community validation (independent):**

| Model | VRAM | tok/s | Tester |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Cascade-2-30B-A3B (cache=8) | 7.6 GB | 15.6 | @caiovicentino |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (cache=8) | 8.6 GB | 14.8 | @caiovicentino |

**LFRU vs LRU** (Nemotron, cache=8): LFRU cache=8 exceeds LRU cache=16 in hit rate. +5.2% speed improvement.

**Unit tests:** 26 test cases (parametrized across dtypes, capacities, num_experts). Tests LFRU-specific eviction behavior (frequency-weighted, not just recency).

## Changes

**15 files, ~810 additions**

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `expert_weight_provider.py` (new) | `CachedWeightProvider` with LFRU eviction, `ExpertWeightResult` dataclass |
| `fused_moe_method_base.py` | `supports_expert_lru_cache` property (default False) |
| `fused_moe_modular_method.py` | Provider check in `apply()` |
| `layer.py` | `_maybe_init_expert_lru_cache()`, `expert_weight_provider` attribute |
| `unquantized_fused_moe_method.py` | CPU weight allocation, cache init, kernel init for cache path, XPU transpose |
| `quantization/fp8.py` | `supports_expert_lru_cache`, provider check, cache init |
| `offload.py` | `moe_expert_cache_size` config field |
| `vllm.py` | Cross-validator: enforce_eager required |
| `arg_utils.py` | CLI argument `--moe-expert-cache-size` |
| `llm.py` | `moe_expert_cache_size` parameter in `LLM.__init__` |
| `basic_correctness.yaml` | CI test area registration |
| `docs/features/moe_cache_policies.md` (new) | Feature documentation |
| `test_expert_lru_cache.py` (new) | 26 unit tests with parametrization |
| `test_moe_expert_cache.py` (new) | Integration test via `compare_two_settings` |
| `benchmarks/qwen_122b_test_20260331.txt` (new) | Benchmark raw data |

## How it works

```text
moe_expert_cache_size == 0 (default):
  No provider created. Zero overhead (one getattr per layer).

moe_expert_cache_size > 0:
  CachedWeightProvider.prepare(topk_ids):
    for each unique expert:
      hit  → update LFRU frequency + recency (O(1))
      miss → evict lowest freq/age score, H2D copy, update mapping
    remap topk_ids → slot indices via persistent GPU mapping tensor
  → kernel receives GPU buffer + remapped IDs
```

## Limitations

- `--enforce-eager` required (CUDA graph compat deferred to PR 2)
- Synchronous H2D copies (async pipeline in PR 2)
- Single eviction policy (LFRU hardcoded, no pluggable framework)
- EP > 1 not supported
- BF16 + FP8 per-tensor only

## Test plan

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_expert_lru_cache.py -v
pytest tests/basic_correctness/test_moe_expert_cache.py -v -s
```

---

*AI-assisted development ([Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)). Architecture validated in [tinyserve](https://github.com/e1n00r/tinyserve).*

items.title: PR Title: [Feature] EWSJF: Adaptive Scheduler for Mixed-Workloads (30-50% Throughput Gain)
items.body:
**Summary**  
This PR introduces EWSJF (Effective Workload‑based Shortest Job First), an adaptive request‑level scheduler designed to eliminate Head‑of‑Line (HoL) blocking in mixed workloads that combine short interactive queries with long batch requests.

The design aligns with RFC #24484 on mitigating HoL blocking and RFC #24484 on pluggable scheduler interfaces.

By grouping requests into performance‑homogeneous queues and applying a density‑weighted scoring function, EWSJF improves both throughput and tail latency compared to the default FCFS scheduler.

**Key Results**  
Benchmarks (Llama‑2‑13B, NVIDIA A100, Poisson arrivals):

- Token Throughput: +30% to +54%  
- TTFT (Short Requests): Up to 4× reduction  
- GPU Utilization: ~65% → ~80%

Full technical report: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21758

**Implementation Details**  
EWSJF runs upstream of the execution engine and includes:

- Refine‑and‑Prune Partitioning: Dynamically groups requests by prompt length to avoid oversized queues.  
- Context‑Aware Scoring: Balances urgency, fairness, and SJF‑style efficiency.  
- Bayesian Meta‑Optimizer: Continuously tunes scoring weights based on workload shifts.

**Test Plan**  
A new benchmark script (`benchmarks/benchmark_ewsjf.py`) simulates mixed workloads.

Reproduction steps:

```
# 1. Generate mixed dataset (80% short, 20% long)
python tools/generate_workload.py --type mixed --count 10000

# 2. Run benchmark with EWSJF
python benchmarks/benchmark_serving.py --scheduler ewsjf --dataset mixed_workload.json
```

**Checklist**

[x] My code follows the style guidelines of this project.  
[x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works.  
[x] I have added necessary documentation (if appropriate).

items.title: [Core][Scheduler] Batch small prefill chunks under decode load
items.body:
## Review summary

- Default-off, text-only scheduler policy; existing behavior is unchanged when `--min-prefill-chunk-tokens=0`.
- Batches sub-threshold prefill chunks only while decode work is runnable, with a bounded delay and cleanup on schedule/abort/finish/preemption.
- Targets long-prompt mixed prefill/decode workloads where the objective is to maximize stable per-GPU QPS under an average E2E latency budget.
- In controlled single-GPU RTX PRO 5000 experiments with the policy predecessor, enabling Small Prefill reduced average E2E from 2.931s to 2.388s at QPS 12 (-18.5%) in one fixed configuration, and moved the stable <=3s capacity knee from 11 to 13 QPS (+18.2%) in another.
- Timeline analysis showed context tokens per step increasing from 1,669 to 4,785, while incremental prefill GPU time fell from 15.069 to 8.788 us/token (-41.7%).
- Focused scheduler/CLI tests and changed-file pre-commit pass; the policy lineage is also operating on approximately 1,600 RTX PRO 5000 workers.

## Purpose

Decode-heavy workloads can leave small text prefill chunks in the remaining
token budget. Launching those chunks individually may underutilize the GPU.

This PR adds an opt-in scheduler policy that:

- defers text prefill chunks smaller than `--min-prefill-chunk-tokens` while
  decode work is runnable;
- releases deferred chunks when their combined size reaches that threshold or
  `--max-prefill-chunk-delay-steps` expires;
- clears pending state on schedule, abort, finish, and preemption; and
- excludes multimodal requests.

The feature is disabled when `--min-prefill-chunk-tokens=0` (the default), so
the existing scheduling path is unchanged by default.

### Duplicate-work check

I searched open PRs for the CLI names and for small-prefill/deferred-prefill
batching and found no implementation of this policy.

Two adjacent policies use different control signals:

- #54627 applies `prefill_schedule_interval` to single-engine runs. It defers
  all prefills on a fixed cadence to protect decode interactivity.
- This PR is size-aware: it defers only sub-threshold text chunks and releases
  them by aggregate tokens or bounded per-request age. It targets batching
  efficiency under an E2E capacity budget.

They are not duplicates. If both are eventually composed, precedence should be
defined because the cadence gate currently runs before this PR's threshold/age
check. They should not be enabled together by default without an interaction
benchmark.

The adjacent P-PAS RFC (#52906) controls the aggregate prefill token budget
under pressure, whereas this PR keeps global budgets unchanged and batches
sub-threshold chunks. A controlled 2x2 experiment found that these policies are
also not universally additive.

### AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with porting the implementation to current `main`, test
drafting, and the upstream overlap audit. I reviewed every changed line,
understand the implementation and validation, and can defend the change.

This changes scheduling timing without changing kernels, token accounting, or
sampling. The TTFT trade-off is documented below.

## Test Plan

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu uv run --active --no-project python -m pytest \
  --confcutdir=tests/v1/core tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
  -k small_prefill -v

VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu uv run --active --no-project python -m pytest \
  --confcutdir=tests/engine tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py \
  -k small_prefill -v

.venv/bin/pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD
```

The scheduler tests cover aggregation, bounded delay, no-decode behavior,
default-off behavior, abort/preemption cleanup, allocation failure, and config
validation.

## Test Result

- Small-prefill scheduler tests: `8 passed`
- CLI parsing test: `1 passed`
- Changed-file pre-commit: all hooks passed, including ruff, formatting, mypy,
  Markdown lint, and config validation

An exploratory full scheduler-file run in the reused minimal CPU environment
reached `122 passed`; 36 multimodal/EC tests could not run because the optional
`mistral_common` dependency was absent. The focused tests above completed
cleanly, and upstream CI has the complete test dependency set.

### SLA-oriented serving validation

The primary use case is not maximum QPH with a relaxed latency target. It is
long-prompt mixed prefill/decode serving where the objective is the highest
stable per-GPU QPS satisfying all of the following:

- average E2E latency <=3s;
- completed QPS keeps up with offered QPS;
- no failures, OOMs, core dumps, or restarts; and
- running and waiting requests do not grow persistently.

The controlled workload used a single RTX PRO 5000 72GB GPU, a Qwen3.5-0.8B
model, TP=1, non-streaming open-loop requests, and a production-derived request
distribution averaging about 5.4K prompt tokens and 300 output tokens. MTP was
disabled; chunked prefill, an 8,192-token batch budget, and FP8 KV cache were
enabled.

The following comparisons changed only Small Prefill within each fixed
configuration:

| Comparison | Fixed configuration | Result |
|---|---|---|
| C -> F | BF16 LM Head + FP8 KV | At QPS 12, average E2E fell from 2.931s to 2.388s (-18.5%); the stable <=3s knee remained at 12 QPS. |
| D -> E | FP8 LM Head + FP8 KV | The stable <=3s knee moved from 11 to 13 QPS (+18.2%). E at QPS 13 measured 2.661s and 2.700s across two GPUs; QPS 14 measured 3.408s and 3.528s and failed the SLA. |

Timeline analysis explains the gain: context tokens per step increased from
1,669 to 4,785 (2.87x), raw context GPU time fell from 16.699 to 9.390 us/token,
and incremental prefill GPU time fell from 15.069 to 8.788 us/token (-41.7%).

These controlled measurements used the production predecessor of this policy.
The PR retains the threshold/delay behavior while hardening per-request age and
lifecycle cleanup. A separate run of the hardened implementation at `3072/384`
sustained QPS 12 at 2.462s average E2E with no failures, preemptions, or
sustained waiting; QPS 13 measured 3.096s. That later baseline was not a fully
matched crossover, so it is supporting reproduction rather than the main
capacity-delta claim.

### Production validation

This policy lineage is currently deployed in a production serving cluster with
approximately 1,600 single-GPU NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 workers and is serving live
traffic. The production configuration uses:

- `--min-prefill-chunk-tokens 3072`
- `--max-prefill-chunk-delay-steps 192`

At the time of verification, all allocated workers were ready and available.
This operational deployment is separate from the controlled `3072/384`
experiments. It demonstrates production-scale operational viability, but is
not used to claim a fleet-wide capacity or latency improvement.

### Interaction with adjacent prefill policies

In a separate peak-throughput 4B experiment, Small Prefill alone improved
QPH/GPU by 1.90%, while combining it with P-PAS was 7.06% below Small Prefill
alone. This is an interaction warning, not the primary performance claim. Both
policies gate prefill admission, so the tested combination is not recommended
without workload-specific validation.

Documentation for both CLI options and the TTFT trade-off is included.
